paragraphs: The largest data center proposed in Colorado is Vantage Data Centers' Trident campus in Aurora: two buildings on 143 acres across the street from new housing, with 334 megawatts of computing capacity and about 500 megawatts of total power demand. Aurora says city staff can approve it without a public hearing because the land is zoned industrial, while state air regulators expect Vantage to hold at least one community meeting before it applies for an air permit. In Colorado Springs, the City Council will decide on Raeden's Project Taurus on April 13, 2027.

About four miles from Trident, QTS is finishing the second of three buildings on its Aurora campus, which will need at least 160 megawatts; it has 40 diesel backup generators and has applied to add 98. Aurora's council voted down a six-month moratorium in August, then unanimously banned evaporative cooling in data centers on September 14. "We are in yet another drought and cannot afford to waste our water resources on a data center," resident Chad Johnson told the council.

Weld County commissioners voted 5-0 on September 9 to approve Global AI's data center at the former Carestream Health site near Windsor, starting at 27.5 megawatts, after more than 400 written comments, mostly opposed. In north Denver, CoreSite's first building in Elyria-Swansea is nearly complete, but Denver's moratorium keeps it from applying for the other two. Douglas County approved a $19 million tax rebate over 35 years for Flexential's data center in Parker, expected to create 16 jobs.

Project Taurus would turn a former Intel chip plant on Garden of the Gods Road into a data center using about 50 megawatts; neighbors have pressed the city about low-frequency noise. The council voted 7-2 on September 17 to delay its decision on residents' appeal until April 13, 2027, one week after the city election.

Alberta is where Canada's biggest data centers are being planned, and the province is courting them. The largest announced so far is Meta's $13 billion, one-gigawatt data center in Sturgeon County, north of Edmonton, announced July 8, 2026 and powered by a new gas plant from 2030. Near Grande Prairie, Kevin O'Leary's proposed $70 billion, 7.5-gigawatt Wonder Valley park got a provincial industrial zone designation on August 26 but still needs its permits. From December 31, grid-connected data centers of 75 megawatts or more pay a 2% levy on their computer hardware.

Sturgeon County had made data centers a permitted use in 2025, so no public vote was needed; hundreds protested in Morinville on August 2. "We don't want this data centre here, and we don't want this data centre anywhere else," said organizer Ben Baril. Greenview's council allowed data centers after a six-minute hearing in November 2024, weeks before Wonder Valley was announced. The Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation is suing the province over a water license for the project; a judge refused in August to throw the case out.

Other places have said no. On August 17 the Alberta Utilities Commission denied Synapse's 1.4-gigawatt gas plant for a 10-building campus in Olds, about 30 meters from homes: "The site is simply not suitable for the proposed development." Rocky View County, next to Calgary, rejected a 448-hectare campus near Balzac 6-1 in September 2025 and in July 2026 paused new data center rezoning applications until it adopts rules, expected this fall. It has approved zoning for a Beacon AI Centers project near Indus.

The grid is the limit. The province's grid operator capped new large loads at 1,200 megawatts until 2028 after 29 projects asked for more than 16 gigawatts, and the province is favoring developers that bring their own power. At a packed town hall in Lacombe on August 19, Technology Minister Nate Glubish was booed and promised setback rules to keep data centers away from homes. "It's delightful to hear those words but absolutely useless after all these months," said Olds opponent Bek MacIntosh.

Beijing has spent more than a decade pushing ordinary data centers out of the city while building government-backed AI computing centers inside it. In 2015 it banned new data centers in six central districts (Dongcheng, Xicheng, Chaoyang, Haidian, Fengtai and Shijingshan). Now it is building four public AI computing centers, in Haidian, Chaoyang, Yizhuang and the Mentougou-Shijingshan area in the west. The next change lands on existing sites: from 2026 the city charges extra for power at data centers that miss its efficiency limit.

That rule comes from a November 2024 city plan to clean up what it calls an "old, outdated, small and scattered" stock of data centers. Sites using 5 million kilowatt-hours a year or more must meet an efficiency ratio of 1.35, meaning at most 35% extra power for cooling and other overhead, and the city wants its average there by 2027. Those over the limit pay 0.2 yuan more per kilowatt-hour on the excess, or 0.5 yuan for the worst. Retrofits can earn grants of up to 30 million yuan.

Much of the capacity squeezed out went next door to Hebei, to Zhangbei, Huailai and Langfang, and to Tianjin, S&P Global's 451 Research reported. Inside the city, the Beijing AI Public Computing Platform, begun in September 2023, expanded again in March 2025, and the Beijing Digital Economy Computing Center opened in April 2025 running mostly on Chinese-made chips. The city's economy bureau says Beijing grew its AI computing supply by more than a third in the first half of 2026.

Seattle's City Council voted 9-0 on June 9, 2026, for a one-year moratorium on new data centers over 20 megavolt-amperes, after Seattle City Light said four companies had approached it about five data centers totaling 369 megawatts, about a third of the city's average daily use. One of those, a 20-megawatt data center that Colossus Data Center Advisors proposed for a former Amazon Fresh store inside the Starbucks Center in SoDo, was sized to stay just under the ban's threshold. Sabey Data Centers withdrew a separate 68-megawatt request at its Tukwila campus.

The vote followed a fierce public response. Residents organized by 350 Seattle, Troublemakers and the Seattle chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America sent emails that councilmembers said topped 98,000, citing strain on a power grid Seattle City Light itself said would struggle with that much new load, plus water use during a state drought emergency. "These communities should not be treated as sacrifice zones," Rebecca Young told a council committee, arguing new sites would likely land in South Seattle and Tukwila neighborhoods that already carry industrial pollution.

The city's roughly 30 existing data centers, including Sabey's 54-megawatt Tukwila campus and Digital Realty's colocation site in the Westin Building downtown, can each expand by up to 20 MVA under the moratorium. Digital Realty also filed plans 11 days before the vote for a data center at a former Bed Bath & Beyond site downtown; whether its earlier paperwork lets that project proceed anyway may end up with permitting officials or the courts.

Seattle City Light's new rate rules for any customer seeking 10 megavolt-amperes or more, adopted in July, apply across its full service area, including Tukwila, Burien, SeaTac and unincorporated King County. The city must hold a public hearing on the moratorium and expects permanent zoning rules in early 2027; a state bill requiring data centers to disclose their environmental impact died without a Senate vote this year.

Middlesex County's biggest data center fight ended in under two weeks. In February 2026, New Brunswick residents learned the city's redevelopment plan for 100 Jersey Avenue, a 22-acre former industrial site near Rutgers and a middle school, had been written to allow a data center alongside about 600 apartments. Hundreds packed City Hall on February 18, and the City Council removed data centers from the plan and restored a public park, passing the change unanimously. "Many people did not want this in their neighborhood," said Bruce Morgan, president of the New Brunswick NAACP.

Sayreville has since adopted its own pause. The Borough Council advanced an 18-month moratorium, Ordinance 15-26, on June 15; a push to make it permanent failed 3-3, with Mayor Kennedy O'Brien breaking the tie against it over the risk of lawsuits. After a July 20 hearing, the moratorium took effect and runs through January 2028. Residents raised noise, water use and tax-break doubts; the Carpenters Union spoke for the construction jobs. No project is pending, though the mayor has pointed to the 400-acre former Hercules site as a likely target.

Old Bridge is still weighing its own ban. Councilman David Merwin's proposed three-year moratorium drew a heated response at a June 9 meeting, so the council instead asked for an ordinance barring data centers in every zoning district. "It turned into a big hullabaloo," Merwin told News 12. Mayor Debbie Walker noted data centers already aren't a permitted use townshipwide, though two redevelopment plans allow them, and a redeveloper called the site's power supply insufficient.

One Middlesex project has already been approved: the South Brunswick Planning Board cleared a 341,000-square-foot data center at the old Princeton Nurseries site in 2025, and residents have since petitioned to reject or suspend it. Mayor Charles Carley says the approval requires sound walls and daytime-only generator testing, and that PSE&G must confirm it can deliver the power requested. Old Bridge's council has not yet scheduled a final vote on its prohibition ordinance.

The Colorado Springs City Council will decide on April 13, 2027 whether Project Taurus, a 50-megawatt AI data center, can go ahead. California-based Raeden wants to convert a former Intel chip plant off Garden of the Gods Road, west of Centennial Boulevard, beside the Chelsea Glen neighborhood. City planners approved the plan in June and the Planning Commission upheld it in July with a 50-megawatt power cap, but two groups appealed to the council. On September 17 the council voted 7-2 to put off its decision until a week after the April city election.

At 50 megawatts, Taurus would be by far Colorado Springs Utilities' largest customer; the utility's biggest data center customer today uses about six. Neighbors fear the low hum that the city's noise rules, written in dBA, do not measure. "We wouldn't be saying no to data centers. We'd be saying no to this data center at this location," Councilman Dave Donelson said. Raeden's lawyer, Caitlin Quander, answered: "This is not a referendum on data centers." Police made several arrests at the September meeting after a resident took up a megaphone.

In August Mayor Yemi Mobolade issued six data center standards requiring large projects to pay for the power infrastructure they need and to protect the city's water supply. North of the city, Monument voted on July 20, 2026 for a six-month moratorium, the first in El Paso County, though no project has applied. Novva Data Centers runs a smaller data center in Colorado Springs, bought at 6 megawatts with plans to grow it to 30.

Granite Renewables, a New York company that develops sites for data centers with their own power, has been talking with Logan County officials about a campus that could need up to 2 gigawatts of power, about 2,000 megawatts, on some 4,000 acres. The Sterling Journal-Advocate placed the site 21 miles northwest of Sterling, near the Nebraska border. No application has been filed. Under county rules in force since February 17, 2026, it would need a special use permit and a public hearing before the county commissioners.

Andrew Fritzer, who chairs the Logan County Economic Development Corporation, told an October 2025 meeting the project could bring up to a thousand construction jobs, $15 billion of investment and 50 to 100 permanent jobs. That month the commissioners paused data centers, battery storage, solar and wind while they wrote rules; the development corporation's director, Trae Miller, worried the pause sent a negative message to the market. For scale, Colorado Springs Utilities needed a little more than 1 gigawatt at its summer peak in 2024.

The rules cover any data center of 1 megawatt or more. Applicants must notify property owners within a mile, map military installations within a mile, send their plans to wildlife and military agencies for review, and show their water source.

Colorado's largest data center projects are in Aurora. QTS is finishing a three-building campus on 65 acres south of Denver International Airport that will need at least 160 megawatts of power: one building is done, a second is nearly finished and work has started on the third. About four miles north, Vantage Data Centers has proposed Trident, two buildings totaling 861,866 square feet on 143 acres, with about 500 megawatts of total power demand. Because the site is zoned industrial, city staff can approve Trident without a public hearing.

On September 14, 2026 the Aurora City Council unanimously banned evaporative cooling in new data centers to save water; the ban goes to a final vote at the council's next meeting. A zoning change listing where data centers may go is headed to the Planning Commission and then back to the council later this year. In August the council rejected a six-month moratorium proposed by Council member Amy Wiles, whose ward includes the Trident site. "The community response has been overwhelming," she said. "They do not want data centers, period."

QTS has 40 diesel backup generators and has applied to state regulators to add 98 more, fitted with exhaust controls, in an area that already fails federal ozone standards. Its closed-loop cooling uses about 2,400 gallons of water a day. Trident would have 28 diesel generators.

Denver has stopped new data centers until at least May 21, 2027. The City Council voted unanimously on May 18, 2026 for a one-year moratorium on permits and site plans for data centers, which took effect May 21. A working group of residents and experts in utilities, health care and air quality is to be named by the end of October to recommend permanent rules. The pause does not cover CoreSite's DE3 building, already under construction.

CoreSite DE3, at 4900 North Race Street in Elyria-Swansea beside the National Western Stock Show complex, went up without a public hearing because the land was already zoned industrial. Its first building, designed for 18 megawatts of power, was nearly finished in August; two more buildings would need city permits under the new rules. The site is across the street from affordable housing, a park and a health clinic. Its state permit allows 14 diesel generators, and CoreSite says its evaporative cooling will use about 115,000 gallons of water a day on average and 230,000 at peak.

Residents gathered 215 signatures on a good neighbor proposal asking CoreSite for cleaner generators and health monitoring. City Council President Amanda Sandoval apologized in May: "I'm sorry that I did not stop that data center when we were asked for a $9 million tax incentive." Council member Kevin Flynn said it was approved as a "storage and trade" facility, a category "which really doesn't speak to what this facility is."

Monroe Township banned data centers everywhere in town on April 22, 2026, and is now being sued for $300 million by Hexa Builders, which wanted to build a 1-million-square-foot data center on its roughly 170 acres at 3043 Black Horse Pike, in the Williamstown area. The case is in federal court in Camden, where U.S. District Judge Edward Kiel has yet to rule on Monroe's request to dismiss it.

The township had changed its redevelopment plan in June 2025 to allow data centers on Hexa's land, at a meeting Mayor Greg Wolfe said no residents attended. After warehouses won preliminary approval there in January 2026, residents feared they could become a data center and packed meetings over water, power bills and noise. The April ordinances removed data centers from the Hexa site and banned them township-wide, allowing only server rooms on no more than 2 percent of a property. "The process worked," Wolfe wrote.

Hexa sued on June 5 after the township declared its data center application incomplete on May 12. Its complaint argues that "data centers are a medium of expression" protected by the First Amendment. The township's lawyer, Todd Gelfand, answered that "the fact that data centers support electronic communications does not transform a land-use regulation into a speech restriction." Hexa has asked for its state-law claims to go back to state court.

In East Greenwich Township, American Tower withdrew its plan for a roughly 4-megawatt data storage building on 6.2 acres along Mantua Road in Mount Royal after a petition against it passed 5,800 signatures. Mayor Jim Philbin said the township was one of the first in South Jersey to adopt an ordinance prohibiting future data centers.

Monmouth County's live data center fight is at Bell Works in Holmdel, the former Bell Labs campus that now houses offices, shops and restaurants. On July 21 the Township Committee introduced a ban on data centers; three days later the property's owner, Somerset Development, filed to build a two-story, 40-megawatt data center on the site, replacing an existing building. The committee adopted the ban unanimously on August 11, but the township's attorney says an applicant is generally entitled to the zoning in effect when its application was filed, and a 2013 redevelopment agreement already lists data centers as a permitted use there.

Founder and chief executive Ralph Zucker says the project is small by today's standards, "less than one-tenth the size of the 300-500-plus megawatt hyperscale data centers driving much of the recent public conversation," and "sits in an isolated portion of the property, out of view from surrounding neighborhoods and roadways." Residents raised power use, noise, water and property values at the August 11 meeting. "We were there to cheer the banning of a data center and it was announced, 'Guess what, guys? The data center is coming,'" said Kin Gee of Better Holmdel. Mayor Rocco Impreveduto said the committee cannot comment on an application pending before the Planning Board.

Neighboring towns have banned data centers before any were proposed there. Red Bank and Asbury Park passed bans in June, Neptune Township banned both data centers and immigration detention facilities in July, and Howell's council passed a ban in August after an earlier moratorium. None of those towns had a known project. Middletown's committee introduced its own ban on September 8, with a final vote scheduled for September 21; the vote was scheduled for that date and no result has been published.

What comes next: the Holmdel Planning Board still has to hold hearings on the Bell Works site plan, where the question is whether the pre-ban zoning and the 2013 agreement let the 40-megawatt data center go ahead.

DataOne is building an AI data center for Nebius off South Lincoln and Sheridan avenues in Vineland, and the state has just fined it. On September 22, 2026 the Department of Environmental Protection fined DataOne $1.07 million for installing 62 gas generators, each about 2 megawatts, without air permits, and gave it 45 days, until about November 6, to get permits or stop running them. Nebius, which has a $17.4 billion deal with Microsoft, says the campus can grow to 300 megawatts of power.

Neighbors have complained for months of a constant hum and metallic whine, and filed a class-action lawsuit that says the county health department cited DataOne in March for nighttime noise. "It's just constant. It never goes away," said Andrew Groetsch, who lives less than a mile away. In August the city issued stop-work orders after crews began building a liquefied natural gas tank and moved fuel cells on site before approval. DEP Commissioner Ed Potosnak called the fine "by far the largest ever taken against a data center in New Jersey."

DataOne says the generators are temporary until Bloom Energy fuel cells, which it says are approved, become the permanent power source, and that it will apply for the permits while disagreeing with the finding. The mayor and City Council president back the project, and the city approved a partial tax exemption as part of a five-year plan. DataOne says it will hire more than 200 permanent workers, and it has bought most of the homes a few hundred feet from the site for employees.

Millville, also in Cumberland County, went the other way. Its Board of Commissioners voted on May 19, 2026 to ban data centers, ending a proposed 2.6-million-square-foot campus that would have drawn 1.4 gigawatts, or 1,400 megawatts, at full capacity. The youth-led Climate Revolution Action Network organized residents and farmers against it. Construction in Vineland is due to finish in late December.

Montgomery Township banned data centers outright on June 18, 2026, in the same hearing where E. Kahn Development (EKD), which owns the former Johnson & Johnson campus in Skillman, argued a data center would be the site's best use. The committee adopted Ordinance 26-1779 unanimously that night, banning both data centers and immigration detention centers, citing electricity demand, water use and cooling noise. "Protecting our power supply, our water, our land, and our quality of life is not anti-progress, it is responsible governance," said Mary Reece, who chairs the township's Environmental Committee.

EKD sued on July 31 in Somerset County Superior Court, asking a judge to void the ordinance. Its complaint calls the ban's basis "public hysteria and political attention rather than sound land use planning" and argues the concerns could be handled with rules instead. EKD has not filed a site plan for a data center on the 257-acre campus, which it bought in December 2025 after Kenvue, the J&J spinoff, moved to Summit; an earlier plan for manufacturing and offices was dismissed by the planning board and is being challenged in a separate suit.

Warren Township banned data centers 5-0 the same night, June 18, though officials said no application or plan existed there. "Warren Township's decision to prohibit data centers is about protecting our residents," said Committeeman Daniel Croson, who introduced it. What comes next: EKD's challenge to the Montgomery ban and its earlier suit against the planning board are both pending in Somerset County Superior Court.

Nutley has zoned an 11-acre lot at 275 Kingsland Street, across from the ON3 campus near Cathedral Avenue, for a "major data center." Prism Capital Partners, which owns the former Hoffmann-La Roche campus, won the approval in July 2025, but has announced no further details and has not filed a data center site plan. Newark, the county seat, is weighing a 12-month pause on all data centers.

The zoning replaced a warehouse plan: Prism had applied to build one at 275 Kingsland Street, and agreed to withdraw it in June 2025 when Nutley's commissioners introduced an overlay zone "so that the property can be transformed into a data center or other uses." "With respect to the Kingsland site, the redevelopment plan contemplates a data center being placed there," said township redevelopment counsel Josh Zielinski. About a mile and a half away, at 492 River Road, Nutley already has a 130,000-square-foot data center that GI Partners bought in 2018.

On September 9, 2026 the Newark Municipal Council passed a resolution by North Ward Councilman Anibal Ramos Jr. backing a 12-month moratorium on developing, expanding or converting data centers anywhere in the city, and referred it to the planning board. Large data centers are now allowed in Newark's industrial, airport and port districts. "Before we open the door to large-scale development, Newark needs rules that protect our residents, our neighborhoods and our taxpayers," Ramos said. The pause takes legal effect only if the council adopts it by ordinance.

Hudson County's two largest cities have banned new standalone data centers. The Jersey City Council voted 9-0 on August 19, 2026 to remove data centers from the uses allowed on the city's industrial land, and Bayonne's council passed a 5-0 ban that Mayor Sharon Ashe-Nadrowski signed on August 13. Existing data centers stay, including about five inside downtown Jersey City office buildings, Equinix's campus in Secaucus and CoreWeave's LGA1 in Weehawken, at the mouth of the Lincoln Tunnel.

"Data centers eat up power, drive up utility bills for every ratepayer in this state, and employ almost nobody," Jersey City Mayor James Solomon said. Critics came from both sides. The ban still allows data centers inside office or campus buildings, which Councilwoman Eleana Little said "are not the large AI data centers that people around the country are protesting right now." Resident Brenden Clark asked the council to table it, arguing a new state law already keeps ordinary customers from paying for large data centers' power.

Bayonne has no data centers, but in the past year three were proposed, including a large AI data center at the Delta Self-Storage site on New Hook Road. Residents packed council meetings for months, and the ban became the defining issue of the May mayoral election, which Ashe-Nadrowski's slate swept after she promised to outlaw them. "We showed that the people can fight back and that we're the ones who have power, not the developers," said resident Jennah Reddick, who led the fight.

Spokane County has one operating data center on record, TierPoint's site in Liberty Lake, and two much larger projects working their way through county government. Avista, the region's utility, signed a memorandum with an unnamed company seeking up to 500 megawatts in north Spokane County before pausing talks on June 12 over ratepayer and environmental concerns. A second proposal, a data center called Rock Point or Big Rock tied to County Commissioner Al French and Apricus Energy, is seeking 1,000 megawatts on 514 acres in the West Plains.

Records obtained by resident Brittany Anderson showed French had worked with Apricus for more than a year before the plan became public; Apricus was formed in 2023 and appeared not to have built anything. "The hydrogen is my goal, not the data center. The data center is ancillary," French said. Residents at a July 30 hearing worried the project would worsen PFAS contamination of West Plains groundwater. "These data centers pollute everything," said Shawna Robinson of Airway Heights. Apricus has since asked Airway Heights to sell it reclaimed water for cooling.

Spokane's city council voted 6-1 on June 22 for a one-year moratorium on data centers over 25 megavolt-amperes, running to June 2027. County commissioners followed on August 18, voting unanimously for a shorter, four-month pause on permits for large-load data centers that runs to December 15, while draft zoning rules go through the planning commission. Those rules would apply to projects over 20 megawatts, steer them to heavy-industrial land, and leave the county's eight already-operating data centers untouched, planning director Scott Chesney has said.

The county planning commission is holding hearings on the zoning rules, which commissioners hope to adopt before the pause expires December 15. At a September 15 hearing, residents again questioned Apricus's legitimacy and French's role in the project.

Kittitas County's data center question centers on Cle Elum, where Blue Fern Development wants to build a $200 million, 100,000-square-foot data center near Interstate 90, drawing 20 megawatts of power and creating up to 40 jobs. Cle Elum's city council passed an emergency six-month moratorium on data center applications on July 31, 2026, three days after Blue Fern's plans were unveiled, and Kittitas County commissioners followed with their own six-month moratorium on August 10. County commissioners held a public hearing on September 15 on extending their moratorium by another six months; no result of that hearing has been published.

Residents pressed the city over water and power. "Is it possible to have a data center here that is not going to hurt us? I don't know yet," said Councilmember Beth Williams. Longtime resident John Carlson said data centers "take a lot of electricity and power that we need to sustain our regular usage." Blue Fern says the project would use closed-loop cooling needing about 80,000 gallons of water in its first year, after which the coolant would be recirculated.

The moratoriums may not stop Blue Fern's project. Its site is covered by a development agreement the city approved in 2002, and attorneys are still deciding whether a data center counts as a use already allowed under it. "Anybody in the city can be as mad as they can be, and they can come and yell at a council that has no power over those things," Councilmember Steven Harper said. Cle Elum's moratorium runs to January 31, 2027; Kittitas County's runs to February 10, 2027, unless extended.

No data center has been proposed in Bergen County, but one site is being marketed for it. In August 2026 Fair Lawn residents found a leasing flyer for the former Nabisco cookie plant on Route 208, billed as "Gateway North 208," that listed "data center by right" and "240 MW of power." The owner, Greek Real Estate Partners, holds Planning Board approval from 2023 only for a 644,000-square-foot warehouse, and there is no data center application; any new plan would have to go back to the Planning Board.

"To be clear, those approvals do not authorize a data center at the property, and there are no pending applications before the borough for a data center at the site," said Mayor Cristina Cutrone, adding that the borough has "no interest in making Fair Lawn a destination for data centers." Still, data centers are one of the uses the redevelopment agreement between the borough and the developer permits. The site, zoned restricted industrial, sits near the Glen Rock border with a school and homes nearby.

Managing partner David Greek said the flyer was about four months old and the company would build the approved warehouse if it finds a tenant. "While we're waiting to find a tenant for that site, we're continuing to investigate alternative uses in case we need to pivot," he said. "We are not changing any of the existing approvals with the town at this moment." Across New Jersey, activists counted 93 towns that had banned data centers by early September 2026.

East Windsor has paused new data centers until December 31, 2027. In June 2026 the township adopted Ordinance 2026-06, an 18-month moratorium on further data center development while it waits for state review and regulation. The township already has one: QTS has run a data center there, first built by McGraw-Hill, for about 12 years, and plans for a second data center on the same site had been approved.

That expansion, and a redevelopment ordinance that could have allowed a data center at Probasco Road and Wykoff Mills Road, drew a wave of community concern. "There are a large number of public concerns and questions in our communities, many of which require statewide guidance and regulations," said Mayor Janice Mirinov. The ordinance asks the state to make big energy users pay their own energy costs rather than homeowners, to require public reporting of energy and water use, and to set standards for noise, heat and emissions.

Elsewhere in the county, officials say no one has asked. Hopewell Township allows data centers only as part of another permitted use, like the one serving the Princeton West Innovation Campus, built for Bristol-Myers Squibb. Princeton's council president said AI data centers have not come before the council. In West Windsor, an online listing suggests Switch is considering a 150-megawatt data center campus, but Mayor Marathe said he had never heard of it and no permits have been filed.

Benton County's main data center proposal is tied to a fertilizer plant. Atlas Agro North America, a Swiss startup, plans a $1.5 billion "low-carbon" fertilizer plant called Pacific Green on 150 acres in north Richland, land it has a $9 million deal to buy from the Port of Benton. In 2025 it added a $500 million data center complex next door, saying the data center would help make the fertilizer plant feasible by sharing costs. In December 2025 the City of Richland granted Atlas Agro a one-year option to buy nearly 275 city-owned acres nearby for $24 million. The projects would share a Bonneville Power Administration substation that the council voted in July to design, contingent on Atlas Agro covering its full $51 million cost; the company has not disclosed how or where it will source power.

Residents have used council public comment for months to try to stop the project, organized through a Facebook group, Tri-Cities Wa Citizens Concerned About Data Centers. The day after Pasco's city council adopted a six-month data center moratorium, nearly a dozen Richland residents spoke against data centers at a July 21 meeting even though none was on the agenda. Kayla Madsen said the city seemed to break the Atlas Agro question into small pieces to make it "sweet and palatable." City Manager Jon Amundson said Richland could not follow Pasco: "Because an option agreement is in effect, imposing a moratorium is not possible," he said, "but that does not mean the city intends to proceed without safeguards."

Two other data centers are being explored nearby: Trammell Crow Company is studying a 500-to-1,000-acre site at Lewis & Clark Ranch in West Richland, and Battelle has sought information on a small secure AI data center at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory in Richland, needing 2 megawatts of power at first and possibly 40 later.
Atlas Agro's option on the Richland land runs to about December 2026, when it must decide whether to sign a purchase agreement that would go to the City Council.

Walla Walla County is in line for Amazon's biggest Eastern Washington data center project. Port commissioners voted unanimously on February 12, 2026 to sell 553 acres of the Wallula Gap Business Park to Amazon Web Services, which plans a $5 billion complex of 16 data centers built in four phases. On September 12 Amazon Data Services filed a land-use application for the first piece, the Amazon Attalia Data Center Campus, on 134 acres along Sundance Road: three 220,000-square-foot data centers, a security building, an industrial water facility and space for a future substation.

The county has deemed the application complete and opened public comment until October 12. Amazon has declined to be specific about the project's energy use; at an August 11 open house, its representatives said the campus would power AI and cloud computing, which College Place resident Rikki Wescott said contradicted earlier claims that it was not an AI data center. Opposition has organized as the Walla Walla Anti-Data Center League, which is asking for a one-year countywide moratorium. "People are actually in a state of panic right now," Robynn Snow said of the water demand at a September 14 commission meeting.

All three commissioners have refused a pause. "If a company is able to acquire water rights, acquire power, acquire land in our industrial zone, and wishes to put in a data center, I say keep them coming," said Commissioner Todd Kimball. Commissioner Gunner Fulmer said the county cannot treat one business differently from others that cause light and noise, and that the state environmental review would answer impact questions. Walla Walla already has small data centers run by Vivio Technologies, Fusion Connect and PocketiNet. After the comment period closes October 12, comments go to Amazon and the county's Community Development Department, before a final decision on the Attalia campus.

Snohomish County's only tracked data center is Centersquare's colocation facility on Highway 99 in Lynnwood, an operating site with 17.3 megawatts of utility capacity. There is no large new project proposed in the county right now, but on June 24, 2026 the County Council still adopted Emergency Ordinance 26-026, a six-month hold on new data center applications anywhere in unincorporated Snohomish County. It covers any facility with a planned electrical load of 2 megawatts or more and runs until it expires or is renewed after a hearing.

"The purpose of the moratorium is to press 'pause' so that our county has the ability to carefully deliberate on what a long-term data center policy should look like," wrote Councilman Nate Nehring, its sponsor. Edmonds resident Joan Smith warned of thin snowpack and drought risk to water supplies, while Charles Burgess of the Laborers' International Union said his union did not oppose the pause but wants any future data center to meet apprenticeship and labor standards. The council held its required public hearing on August 19; the moratorium expires December 25, 2026 unless renewed.

Marysville's city council passed its own six-month moratorium on July 13, 2026 while it finishes water and sewer studies. "We're not saying 'no' to data centers," council member Kelly Richards said. "We're just trying to figure out what we are actually willing to accept." Arlington clarified in June that its code does not allow data centers, after a rumored project called Project Cascade turned out to be an unrelated Amazon facility.

Snohomish PUD treats any customer over 2.5 megawatts as a large load, requires a costly system impact study before connecting new developments, and says it would have to secure new power supply for any large data center. "We're not pro or anti-data center. Our goal is to be pro-local," said Chief Customer Officer John Hoffman. Local reporting has also pointed to a Ziply Fiber facility near Paine Field, drawing about 1.1 megawatts, as one of the county's few existing data centers, though it doesn't appear in the tracked list above.

Passaic County's one tracked data center is CyrusOne's NYM2 site in Totowa, an older colocation facility, a data center where multiple companies rent space, at 50 Madison Road. No new data center has been proposed in the county.

The nearest new proposal sits just over the line in Clifton and Nutley. Prism Capital Partners' ON3 campus, the former Hoffmann-La Roche headquarters on Route 3, won redevelopment approvals from both towns in 2025: a Clifton plan for housing, shops and a neighborhood market, and a Nutley plan letting an 11-acre parcel at 275 Kingsland Street host "a major data center and other permitted uses." Together the approvals allow up to 1,074 homes, about 90,000 square feet of retail, a research building and the data center.

No Passaic town has introduced a data center ban, and no hearing is scheduled here. Any data center on the ON3 campus would go before Nutley's planning board, since the data center parcel sits on the Nutley side of the line.

St. Charles County's fight started with Project Cumulus, a $1 billion AI data center campus that CRG pitched on 440 acres near the City of St. Charles's water wells in August 2025. After residents packed City Hall over water and diesel fuel concerns, the city adopted a moratorium and CRG withdrew its permit application. On May 19, 2026, the council voted 7-1 to ban large-scale data centers outright, while still allowing server rooms at hospitals, schools and companies.

"We have peace, at last," said resident Rodolfo Salazar, who would have lived within a mile of the site. St. Peters and Wentzville have also each adopted their own data center moratoriums. On July 13, the county council unanimously approved a six-month, countywide moratorium on data centers over 100,000 square feet or 5 megawatts, though no proposal was pending at the time. County Executive Steve Ehlmann said, "let's do the moratorium, let's find out what the facts are."

The county moratorium runs through mid-January 2027 unless the council extends it; Missouri law caps such pauses at six months at a time. Ehlmann said the county is watching data center proposals in nearby Franklin and Montgomery counties.

Meta was behind a $1 billion data center proposed for 1,077 acres of farmland in Howell Township, developed through Stantec Consulting Michigan and landowner Randee LLC, trustee Bob Wilson told Michigan Advance and MLive in November 2025. The Van Gilder family, which owns the land, withdrew its rezoning request in December 2025, the night before a scheduled hearing, after the township and county planning commissions both voted against it. Township officials had adopted a six-month moratorium on new site plans that November, though it did not cover rezoning.

Residents organized as Stop the Data Centers Livingston County and gathered more than 3,700 petition signatures. Hundreds packed a seven-hour township meeting on September 23, 2025, and emails later showed officials had signed nondisclosure agreements with the developers. Ryan Van Gilder wrote to officials from a DTE Energy-arranged bus tour of Ohio data centers, "If your meeting gets postponed on Sept 23 you guys are dead." The family's withdrawal statement said it would "honor the current moratorium," but resident Breanne Green, who obtained the emails, said, "This is far from over."

Tyrone Township, elsewhere in the county, has had its own moratorium on new data centers in place since December 2, 2025, with no end date set. Howell Township's moratorium was due to run about six months from November 2025; no result on new township rules, or on whether the Van Gilder family has resubmitted its rezoning request, has been published.

Dane County's data center fight began in the town of Vienna north of Madison, where QTS Data Centers proposed a campus in late 2025 on land that would have been annexed into the village of DeForest. The land is still designated for agricultural preservation in the county's comprehensive plan, and American Transmission Company filed in December for a permit to expand a substation in Vienna to "provide electrical service to a potential new customer." DeForest paid Mueller Communications about $109,000, to be reimbursed by QTS, to handle public relations around the proposal. Residents organized against it, and on February 3, 2026 the DeForest Village Board voted unanimously to reject the annexation petition; the substation application was withdrawn at the end of January. "And now we are seeing an unprecedented number of new 'sacrifice zones' being created across the United States, and even here in Wisconsin," said Winona Storms, an organizer of the opposition. County Board member Colin Barushok said a QTS executive told him DeForest's rejection had deterred the company from exploring further projects in the county.

The proposal prompted County Board Chair Patrick Miles to set up an advisory committee on data centers, which began meeting in February, to "lift the veil of opacity" he had seen elsewhere. He had wanted a countywide moratorium too, but county lawyers said state law prohibited it. Then Manitowoc County passed one by targeting the permitting process rather than development itself, and Dane County copied it. On June 4, 2026 the County Board unanimously approved a pause on zoning permit applications for hyperscale data centers until December 2027 in the 26 towns under county zoning. It does not cover the six towns that have opted out of county zoning, or the county's villages and cities, which zone for themselves. Supervisor Aria Trucios, a power plant operator, compared a data center's uneven load on the grid to a "brick in a dryer."

The City of Madison adopted its own one-year moratorium in January 2026 while planners write data centers into the zoning code; the city has no hyperscale data centers but many small and colocation ones. Madison's planning director confirmed the city had heard from Cloverleaf, the start-up that brokered land and power for Microsoft's Mount Pleasant campus and Vantage's Port Washington project, about a data center on the far east side.

The advisory committee is still working through water, energy and economic effects and is expected to report in about May 2027, and the county has until December 2027 to write data centers into its zoning ordinance and comprehensive plan. Madison's moratorium runs to January 2027.

Lancaster County's data center story is in the City of Lancaster, where two former R.R. Donnelley/LSC Communications printing plants are becoming what may be the largest investment in the county's history. Machine Investment Group paid $130 million in early 2025 for the plants at 216 Greenfield Road near Route 30 and 1375 Harrisburg Pike next to Long's Park, 144 acres in all. In July 2025, at Sen. Dave McCormick's Pennsylvania Energy and Innovation Summit, CoreWeave announced up to $6 billion for an AI data center there, starting at 100 megawatts with room for 300, co-developed by Chirisa Technology Parks and Machine Investment Group with CoreWeave as sole tenant. The developers put the two campuses' combined construction cost at $10 billion. CoreWeave projects about 600 construction jobs and 70 permanent roles at launch, rising to 175.

The city had little say over whether it happens. Both sites are zoned Suburban Manufacturing, and the city classified data centers as "wholesale trade and storage," a permitted use. "As long as something complies with the law, even if everyone in town hates it, the municipality will have to approve it," said PennFuture attorney Brigitte Meyer. The first phase at Greenfield Road, a reuse of the existing building, needed no land development approval and is under construction; a resident's appeal of the zoning determination was pending in late 2025. In August 2025 the City Council asked its solicitor to draft a data center zoning ordinance that would require zoning hearings and public input.

Instead of a fight, the city negotiated. On November 20, 2025 the council voted 6-1, with Janet Diaz opposed, to approve a community benefits agreement with Chirisa, over the objections of most of the more than a dozen speakers. It guarantees $20 million, secured by a letter of credit and split between economic development and sustainable development funds; noise no greater than today's at nearby homes and parks; the site's 176 backup diesel generators meeting state and federal air standards and tested only on weekday daytimes; and 100 percent renewable electricity, including nuclear, for the first ten years or millions of dollars in penalties, with operations barred below 60 percent. In return, neither site will be subject to the city's proposed new data center rules if development plans are filed within two years, though the Harrisburg Pike site and Greenfield's second phase still need planning commission approval. "If they meet the requirements of the law, they're going to build the data centers, and you won't have any of the benefits built into this agreement," City Solicitor Barry Handwerger told council. Resident Darrell Lagace called the clean-energy clause "pay to pollute."

Phase two at Greenfield Road, a two-story building of about 735,128 square feet costing up to $2.5 billion including equipment, has gone to the planning commission, according to LNP reporting compiled by a local civic site; the developers say it includes a $200 million PPL substation and switchyard and that each site will use no more than 20,000 gallons of water a day, with air-cooled chillers. In early 2026 the city was seating a five-member Innovation Hub Committee, with a Chirisa or CoreWeave representative among its members, to oversee the $10 million economic development fund. At the state level, the Pennsylvania House voted 104-95 in March 2026 for a bill requiring data centers to pay for grid upgrades and new generation and to meet rising clean-energy shares. What comes next: planning commission review of phase two and of any Harrisburg Pike plans; the phase one building is due for completion in summer 2027.

Meta is building a $10 billion data center campus in Lebanon's LEAP Research and Innovation District: 13 buildings on 1,500 acres, 10 of them data centers, with the first phase expected online in late 2027 or early 2028. Everywhere else, Boone County has paused new data centers: the County Commissioners unanimously adopted a one-year moratorium on June 15, 2026, running through June 15, 2027, for unincorporated land and the town of Advance. It does not affect Meta.

LEAP is a state-sponsored technology park on land annexed into Lebanon, so the county has little say over it. Water use in the district, which also holds Eli Lilly plants, has been at the heart of the local debate. The state granted Meta a 35-year sales tax exemption for investing at least $1 billion in its first six years. Meta says it will pay the full cost of its energy, give $1 million a year for 20 years to the Boone REMC Community Fund for energy bill help, and "restore 100%" of the water it uses through a farm irrigation project.

The moratorium covers about 60 percent of the county's land, where no data center had been proposed. "We just want to get ahead of these projects that might encroach on the rural lifestyle and rural atmosphere," said Area Plan Commission president John Merson, who has said he would rather ban them. All four speakers at the June 3 hearing supported a pause. "I'd rather you just say no more to begin with and not even mess with a year," said Thorntown resident Cynthia Holmes.

The county's zoning code dates from 1998 and its comprehensive plan from 2009, and neither was written with modern data centers in mind. County planners are using the moratorium year to study them as part of updating both, before the pause ends June 15, 2027.

Hendricks County has two data center projects. In Pittsboro, Vantage Data Centers won approval in March 2025 to rezone 626 acres of farmland north of Interstate 74 and west of County Road 500 East, where it plans a campus of three buildings on about 285 acres using 256, 96 and 48 megawatts of power. In Plainfield, RadiusDC's plan for two 100,835-square-foot buildings on 31 acres at Smith Road and AllPoints Parkway, a 24-megawatt campus, was approved by the Plan Commission in January 2026.

Pittsboro's Town Council approved the rezoning 5-0 without taking public comment, after the plan commission recommended it 4-1 before an overflow crowd. "It's gonna be a complete nuisance," said Donald Brophy, who lives across the street. "We've got one stoplight." Council President Jarod Baker said Steel Dynamics, which has a mill in Pittsboro, had raised "a rightful concern" about whether the local grid could serve both. Vantage plans to rent space to several tenants, and town officials say it will use a low-water cooling method.

In April 2025 Brophy and other neighbors sued the town and Vantage in Hendricks County, saying the town gave improper notice of the annexation and rezoning and required no traffic, environmental or water studies. They asked the court to void both. No ruling in the case has been published.

The Plainfield site was already zoned industrial, so it did not need a Town Council vote. The town says the buildings will use about 700 gallons of water a day, sit more than a quarter mile from the nearest home, and that Duke Energy has confirmed it can supply the power.

Kane County's newest data center proposal is on a farm outside South Elgin. White Rose Partners, a Dallas developer that says it has sited more than 20 data centers, filed a concept plan in July 2026 for Project Kilo, a 200,000-square-foot data center on nine acres of a 20-acre site at 33W304 Kenyon Road, at Kenyon Road and Illinois Route 25 in unincorporated Elgin Township. The land would have to be annexed into South Elgin, and it belongs to Mike Kenyon, 81, a dairy farmer who represented the area on the Kane County Board for 18 years. "It's an ideal place," he said. "No houses, a Prairie Path with row of trees ... as long as village makes them pay for what they use."

White Rose has asked ComEd for 48 megawatts of power. The developer says Project Kilo would pay more than $1 million a year in property taxes, use closed-loop cooling with a one-time fill of less than half an Olympic pool, and pay for all grid upgrades. A Change.org petition against it passed 8,300 signatures by late July, urging officials "to prioritize the needs and wishes of the South Elgin residents over corporate interests." The village postponed its first planning session because it clashed with a summer concert, and the Planning and Zoning Commission's review of the concept plan was later moved off its August 19 date to one not yet set.

Aurora, the county's largest city, has already written rules other towns are watching. It put a 180-day moratorium on new data centers and warehouses in September 2025 and, on March 24, 2026, adopted what CBS Chicago called the strictest data center regulations in the state: lower sound limits, required sound and resource-use studies, and generators at least 1,500 feet from homes. Neighbors of a CyrusOne data center near Interstate 88 still told the council of a constant hum. "I can hear the chiller fans in my yard, I hear it in the shower, I hear it all the time, it never goes away," said Laura Evans. South Elgin's Planning and Zoning Commission has not yet set a new date to take up Project Kilo's concept plan.

TECfusions says the former Alcoa Technical Center in Upper Burrell Township could eventually hold 3 gigawatts of computing power, which would make it the Pittsburgh area's largest data center. The company controls about 1,400 acres it calls Keystone Connect; one building, Building J, is already live and serving an unnamed tenant. Upper Burrell adopted a 180-day moratorium on new data center development in May 2026, but it excluded work already permitted, and on August 5 the supervisors approved a land development plan for Building J's electrical and mechanical upgrades. The moratorium ends November 2, 2026.

Protect PT and two New Kensington residents, Guy Fuller and Allen Uhler, have appealed the August approval to the Westmoreland County Court of Common Pleas, arguing TECfusions should have gone before the zoning hearing board first. "It doesn't look good when you don't answer questions," Fuller told a September 2 meeting attended by more than 50 residents, most of them opposed. "Alcoa brought a lot of good things to this community," said resident David Ostrosky. "Bottom line is, I don't get that vibe from these guys." Vice Chair Kenneth Slahtovsky said the board was learning alongside residents and that nothing was being done yet for the hyperscale project itself.

The township's planning commission was due to review a draft data center ordinance on September 15; no result has been published. Residents want the same ordinance to regulate TECfusions' planned on-site power plants, which Slahtovsky wants handled separately. Neighboring East Deer, Oakmont, Tarentum, Murrysville and Gilpin have also moved to regulate data centers, and a bill letting municipalities adopt their own 180-day pauses awaits the state Senate.

Portage County's cities shut the door on data centers in a single month in spring 2026, triggered by a proposal in Ravenna. Local landowner Ray Harner appeared to plan a data center on his property on State Route 14, across from UH Portage Medical Center, the Portager reported; he declined to comment. City administrators called it no big deal, but at an April 10 meeting residents packed the room. "I can confidently say that there was not one person who was in support of seeing something like this built in the city of Ravenna," said Councilwoman Carmen Laudato. "These things are not economic development," she said. "They are locusts and leeches on our resources. They inflate people's utility costs." On April 20 Ravenna City Council unanimously adopted a 12-month moratorium that also covers server farms and cryptocurrency mining, "to allow for study and development of appropriate legislation."

The county's one project on record is a much bigger one: Bitdeer, a Singapore-based bitcoin miner, and Streetsboro developer Geis Cos. want to build a 750-megawatt, 15-building computing campus on 257 acres at the Turnpike Commerce Center in Shalersville Township, next to the Ohio Turnpike, News 5 Cleveland reported. More than 200 people packed Shalersville's town hall for a meeting that ran three and a half hours, questioning the companies on energy use, water and noise. Shalersville trustees have since extended the township's existing moratorium while they study the plan.

Kent had acted five days earlier. Its council adopted Ordinance 2026-31 on April 15 as an emergency measure, halting permits and applications for data centers for up to a year while the city studies whether it has "the necessary processes, resources and infrastructure," citing data centers' demands on energy, water and infrastructure capacity. On April 27 Streetsboro's council unanimously adopted a one-year moratorium on data centers, crypto mining and "substantially similar uses," making it the fourth Portage community to pause them. "I have no desire to allow them," Streetsboro Mayor Glenn Broska wrote, saying the pause would let the city "draft a defensible and ironclad text amendment that will preclude them from being built in the city." Law Director Joseph Grandinetti noted three or four data center bills pending in Columbus.

Ohio has nearly 200 data centers, most around Columbus, and members of the Facebook group Portage Residents for Responsible Development are circulating petitions for a statewide ballot measure to ban them.

What comes next: the Portage moratoriums run about a year, into spring 2027, while each city writes zoning rules; Streetsboro's mayor has said he wants a permanent ban. Any revival of the Route 14 proposal in Ravenna would face whatever rules the city adopts.

Houston-based Cloverleaf Infrastructure, which prepares land and power for data centers and then finds a company to build on them, has made two proposals in Monroe County. It withdrew its first, the 750-acre Project Ironwood spanning Dundee and Milan townships, in October 2025 after opposition; Dundee Township then adopted a moratorium and extended it six months in January 2026. Its second, Project Cherry Blossom, is a proposed campus on the former River Raisin Golf Course in Frenchtown Township, which the township now owns and Cloverleaf wants to buy.

Residents organized as Protect Frenchtown, and dozens joined a January 18 protest against both projects. Frenchtown's township board adopted a temporary moratorium on data centers on March 10, 2026, with no end date set, while its planning commission reviews it. A recall petition targets Supervisor Al VanWashenova, Treasurer Sheila Bussell and Trustee Julie Ellison over their attendance at a November 2025 Cloverleaf presentation; petitioners had until July 31, 2026 to submit 2,124 valid signatures for each official, and no result has been published.

Cloverleaf says on its project website that Cherry Blossom would bring more than 1,000 construction jobs and closed-loop cooling, and pay for any power upgrades so other DTE customers' rates do not rise; it is negotiating a community benefits agreement with the township. What comes next: the township's final action on its moratorium and any sale of the golf course land to Cloverleaf.

Bulloch County, around Statesboro, has spent 2026 arguing about whether to ban data centers or regulate them. The county government imposed a 90-day moratorium in mid-February on data center zoning anywhere in its unincorporated area. On May 5 commissioners extended it to December 31 and voted 5-0 to start the process of banning data centers outright through a zoning text amendment, which the appointed Planning and Zoning Board recommended. The amendment defined data centers and then excluded them from the General Business, Heavy Manufacturing and Light Manufacturing zones.

Commissioners balked when it came back. They tabled it 3-2 on August 4, and on September 1 voted 4-3 to kill it, with Chairman David Bennett breaking a tie in favor of Commissioner Timmy Rushing's motion to "deny this text amendment, leave the moratorium in effect, and give everybody ample time to figure out what's going on before we put something in permanently." Commissioners Ray Davis and Ray Mosley voted with Rushing; Nick Newkirk, Toby Conner and Anthony Simmons voted to keep the ban alive. "I'll go on the record saying I don't think that this community needs a largescale, 'Meta,' data center," Bennett said. "But at the same time, I'm not going to ignore the fact that by doing an outright ban we'd put ourselves in a potential for legal jeopardy here in this community." Newkirk, who had visited Memphis to see data centers powered by gas turbines, played the commissioners a recording he measured at 60 decibels and noted that data centers run around the clock.

The alternative on the table is regulation. County staff have drafted an ordinance allowing data centers by right only in special overlay districts, with setbacks of at least 350 feet from most neighbors and 500 feet in industrial zones, decibel limits, generators restricted to emergencies and scheduled testing, noise testing before occupancy, downcast lighting, closed-loop cooling and connection to municipal water and sewer. Planning Director James Pope said the main benefit could be lower property taxes, and noted that the county's high-voltage lines limit where data centers could go; only one 230-kilovolt line, the kind Georgia Power prefers, crosses the county. "The intent here is to make sure that they are not put next to a residential neighborhood and that they're not going to go and use up ag land to put a data center on it," Bennett said. Newkirk wanted a way to "shut these places down if they violate our rules."

The city has gone further. On August 18 Statesboro's City Council voted 3-2 to rezone a 26-acre site at the edge of the city on Burkhalter Road for a data center proposed by developers, though no special-use permit application had yet been filed; the county's rules do not apply inside city limits. The county has formed a 21-member working group of residents, three named by each commissioner, to study data centers before the moratorium expires on December 31, and Bennett said it could probably be extended.

Compass Datacenters is building a five-building data center campus on about 350 annexed acres off Stamey Farm Road near Interstate 40, west of Statesville and about 49 miles northwest of Charlotte. The Statesville City Council voted 8-0 in September 2025 to rezone the land for the Dallas-based developer, which has since annexed and approved the site, with power to come from a nearby Duke Energy substation. Compass says the plan calls for five 270,000-square-foot buildings and will employ about 200 people.

The vote came over neighbors' objections: 17 residents urged denial at the hearing and five spoke in favor. "Please do not be swayed by a big carrot of corporate America. Please consider the people that are in this room," said real estate broker Jade Benfield. "I want my grandchildren and children to grow up in a manner I grew up in, where I can swing from an oak tree and breathe clean air," said nurse Sheila Shuford. Compass's Brett Collard said operations "will not burden the (electrical) grid or taxpayers."

A year later, the city changed course for future projects. After a packed August 10, 2026 hearing, the council unanimously approved a 180-day moratorium on new data center applications, adopted on second reading on September 14; the Compass project, already approved, is exempt. The moratorium runs through mid-March 2027 while staff draft new rules, including whether data centers should need case-by-case council approval rather than being allowed by right. The rules go first to the Planning Board, then to the council.

Brown County's data center fight has centered on the village of Wrightstown, population about 3,300, where Cloverleaf Infrastructure, a Houston company, had been talking with village administrator Travis Coenen since at least January 2026 about rezoning land for an AI data center of up to about 1 gigawatt; no site had been identified. On May 27 the Village Board chose to put the question to a referendum rather than pass a policy on its own, and on June 16 it voted a temporary moratorium on data center zoning and planning to hold decisions until after the vote; the village's published moratorium notice lists it running from July 7, 2026 to July 7, 2027.

On August 11 voters delivered a lopsided result: of 1,184 votes cast, 1,033, about 87 percent, said no to the village considering AI data center proposals, and 151 said yes. The referendum is non-binding, but Coenen had said it would have a "huge influence" on the board. Cloverleaf had already dropped a similar project in nearby Greenleaf after officials there said data centers were "off the table."

At the county level, officials say their hands are tied because every town, village and city in Brown County sets its own zoning. Supervisor Christopher Welch proposed a countywide moratorium so municipalities would have "a little bit more teeth," but on June 2 the Planning, Development and Transportation Committee declined to take it up. "So whatever we do here is not going to affect anything," said committee chair Norbert Dantinne, who told residents to seek a moratorium from their own town or village.

Three county supervisors are now surveying local governments and will recommend how the county can help; Wisconsin's legislature left its session without data center rules and does not return until January. Wrightstown's moratorium remains in effect while the board decides how to respond to the referendum result.

CRG, the data center arm of St. Louis builder Clayco, has city approval for a $6 billion data center on about 360 acres north of Highway 67 and west of Highway CC in Festus, but as of June 2026 it had filed no plans or permit requests. No company has been named to run it. The opposition group Wake Up Jeffco and neighbors on Glenkee Court have a lawsuit pending in St. Louis County Circuit Court to stop the project; the defendants have moved to dismiss it.

The Festus City Council annexed and rezoned the land unanimously in November 2025, and on March 30, 2026 voted 6-2 for a development agreement requiring CRG to pay for water, sewer and street upgrades and pay the city $3 million a year for five years, then $5 million a year for five more. Emails released under the Sunshine Law showed council members had met CRG in small groups to avoid a quorum. "I'm against putting data centers between homes," said Lauren Albers, who lives three houses from homes CRG offered to buy.

On April 7 voters replaced four incumbents with candidates who opposed the project. Clayco founder Bob Clark said the approval gave CRG "vested rights" and he hoped to finish in 2028. Residents gathered recall petitions against Mayor Sam Richards and three council members who backed the project, but the council rejected them 4-3 on June 8. "Nobody's backing down," said opponent Lori Merriman.

Powhatan County, a largely residential county west of Richmond, has approved what BizSense called the largest data center project the county has ever had on the table: a campus on Page Road near Anderson Highway, in eastern Powhatan near the Chesterfield County line. Province Group, a developer based in Newport Beach, California, won a 3-2 vote in October 2024 to rezone 119.9 acres from agricultural to light industrial for three data centers totaling about 1.5 million square feet. In October 2025 supervisors voted 5-0 to rezone another 61.8 acres for its affiliate Newport Equities, making a 181-acre campus now marketed by JLL as Powhatan Technology Park. Dominion Energy estimated the full campus at 300 to 400 megawatts of power.

The case for it was tax base. Residential property makes up just over 93 percent of the county's property values, and the board has set a goal of raising commercial property's share of revenue to 15 percent; the county expects about $10 million a year in additional property tax from the campus. "I think this project will be a phenomenal addition to Powhatan and the future of this county," said Vice Chairman Mark Kinney, "especially to really balance out the revenue between commercial and residential."

Getting there was contested. The Planning Commission recommended denying both rezonings; the developer then added proffers to fund utility work, setbacks, buffers and turn lanes on Anderson Highway. Residents and a supervisor objected in 2024 that there was no named end user for the site. "In order to go to market, we need our zoning approval," Province Group CEO Mark Kerslake said. By September 2025 he said an end user had been lined up for the first 120 acres, though it was not named.
What comes next is site plans, which Dominion needs before issuing a formal letter of authorization for the power supply, and the naming of the end user.

Valara Holdings, a NorthMark Strategies subsidiary, is turning the former Kohler kitchen and bath plant on South Pine Street, on 300 acres southeast of Spartanburg, into a $2.8 billion computing center of more than 900,000 square feet. The project became public in March 2025, when the county negotiated tax incentives for a promise of 27 jobs. Construction is under way. The site is permitted for 24 natural gas generators of 2 megawatts each, and the company has asked regulators for more turbines that would raise its generation to about 450 megawatts.

In September 2026, NorthMark Compute and Cloud said the campus would use 1.2 to 1.6 million gallons of water a day, up from an earlier estimate of 459,000. "If you're a baseball player, you could go from my front yard and throw a baseball across the street to their property," said neighbor Karen Eilders.

The Southern Environmental Law Center, backed by residents at a packed Public Service Commission hearing, argued the private power plant needed state siting review. On August 27, 2026, the commission ruled unanimously for Valara, saying the facility will not export power to the grid for public use, so the siting law does not apply. "Companies like Valara can build power plants of any size without any oversight from the commission," said the law center's Kate Mixson. A separate lawsuit filed July 6, 2026, argues the county wrongly classified the project as minor, avoiding Planning Commission review.

The county has moved to stop the next ones. In June it used the pending-ordinance doctrine to freeze applications and block a data center at 300 Jones Road from Lighthouse Data Centers; zoning officials later denied Lighthouse's appeal. In February 2026, TigerDC withdrew its own $3 billion Project Spero from nearby Moore after officials denied its tax deal. On September 21, 2026, the council voted 5-1 for a one-year moratorium on data centers over 65 megawatts; Valara, already permitted, is exempt. Councilwoman Jessica Coker voted no, saying no evidence showed a public safety threat.
Next: a court ruling on Valara's minor classification, the state's decision on its added turbines, and the moratorium's year-long study period.

Lebanon County's first big data center proposal lasted about a month. In April 2026 Inch & Co., through a joint venture with Eastern Land & Resources called 1235 Martina Drive Owner LLC, asked South Annville Township to rezone about 49 acres of commercial land to industrial for a $1.7 billion campus of five data centers on U.S. Route 422 just west of Mount Pleasant Road, beside an already approved 3-million-square-foot DHL complex. Development vice president Joe Eisenhauer described buildings with 50-foot walls, closed-loop cooling with air-cooled chillers, noise of 40 to 50 decibels, 50 to 100 jobs, and a possible deal to use treated effluent from the Annville sewer plant; the plan also required realigning Mount Pleasant Road. The township solicitor had advised that simply banning data centers would be illegal, Eisenhauer said, so the company was helping draft an ordinance.

The opposition came fast. When Eisenhauer briefed county commissioners on April 15, the room was packed mostly with protesters, and chairman Mike Kuhn allowed public comment even though the commissioners have no vote on it. Roberta Gerhart said 3,200 people live within a mile of the site and asked what living near existing data centers has done to people. One South Lebanon resident who had worked in data centers for two decades spoke in favor, citing jobs for young people. The township Planning Commission voted against recommending the rezoning, a petition passed 500 signatures, and in early May the developer's lawyers wrote to the South Annville supervisors that it had "decided to no longer pursue the development of a data center in South Annville Township." One organizer told RealClearPennsylvania's columnist that while many organizers were liberals, many of their supporters were Republicans; the columnist described the meetings as spirited but civil.

Other townships are writing rules instead. On September 14 North Annville Township's supervisors unanimously adopted an ordinance allowing data centers only as a conditional use in its manufacturing district along the railroad and Route 422, on lots of at least 100 acres with no more than half covered, buildings no taller than 50 feet including rooftop equipment, and required traffic and sound studies. "A township can't exclude a use," township solicitor Paul Bametzreider said, adding that "it's unconstitutional to exclude a certain use from your municipality." He said North Lebanon, Union and Jackson townships have written similar ordinances.

At the state level, the Pennsylvania House passed bills in June letting municipalities adopt 180-day data center pauses and ending the data center sales tax exemption, which await the Senate. What comes next: no new data center application in Lebanon County has been publicly reported; the county's townships continue adopting data center ordinances.

LaPorte County's data center story is Microsoft's, and it is centered on the city of La Porte. In 2024 the company announced a 245,000-square-foot data center on 489 acres at the Radius Industrial Park as part of a $1 billion investment in Northwest Indiana. Site preparation began in March 2026; Microsoft told an April 21 community meeting the first buildings would be worked on through the end of 2027 and completed in 2029. At the same meeting it showed a draft plan to expand the site to 17 buildings, seeking to rezone adjacent property.

In May, the La Porte Common Council voted unanimously to annex about 1,000 more acres of farmland and rezone it light industrial, bringing the campus to about 1,300 acres near U.S. 35 and State Road 4. Microsoft told the council it would cover infrastructure costs so residents' electric bills would stay the same, and pointed to a $1 million payment to La Porte schools. Not everyone was consulted: County Commissioner Joe Haney told WNDU the county learned of the annexation from a newspaper notice. "They just published in the newspaper. And that's how we found out about it that day," he said.

The county has since written its own rules for land outside the cities. On May 6, the county commissioners unanimously adopted a data center ordinance limiting data centers to industrial zones and setting standards for setbacks, noise and fire department training. Commissioner Steve Holifield called it only the second standalone data center ordinance in Indiana. Commissioner Connie Gramarossa said the right place for one in the unincorporated county was the Kingsbury Industrial Park, "not something that we want next to somebody's home."

The county's other city is also building one: Google has taken over the Project Maize data center campus planned for Michigan City. Nearby, Microsoft has bought 939 acres in Mishawaka and is pursuing a separate project in Granger, and Amazon Web Services has announced $11 billion for St. Joseph County. Construction of the La Porte campus continues toward its 2029 target, and the county's data center committee is expected to bring back further rule changes.

Effingham County, a county of about 75,000 people outside Savannah, woke up on July 22, 2026 to learn it would host one of the largest data centers in the country. OpenAI announced Project Camellia, a privately funded $20 billion campus of four buildings, about 4.4 million square feet, on a 1,400-acre tract of the Savannah Gateway Industrial Hub near Rincon. Georgia Power will supply 3.2 gigawatts of power in phases from 2028 to 2032 under a 25-year agreement, and OpenAI will provide up to a gigawatt of "flexible demand response" when the grid is strained, Georgia Power spokesman Joshua Peacock told The Current GA. The state's regional review later put peak load at 3,210 megawatts, which WTOC reported would make it the largest single electricity consumer in Georgia history, more than both new reactors at Plant Vogtle. The developer of record is Octans GA LLC, an OpenAI affiliate. OpenAI promised $80 million in community benefits, up to $71 million in Codex credits for Georgia students, 400 permanent jobs, and a closed-loop cooling system; the regional review estimates water use at about 30,000 gallons a day.

The deal was done before the public heard of it. According to The Current GA's reconstruction from records, Georgia Power brokered the first meeting between OpenAI and the county's Industrial Development Authority on Oct. 30, 2025. County officials, including the school superintendent, were briefed in February 2026. Local officials visited OpenAI's Abilene, Texas campus in the spring, and on May 6 OpenAI and Georgia Power representatives met Gov. Brian Kemp in his office. At an April 21 town hall the development authority's chief was reported as saying the agency was not actively considering a data center. The authority then approved the memorandum of understanding unanimously on Tuesday, July 21, at a meeting announced by email to seven people three business days ahead; three OpenAI delegates attended and no one from the public did. The 26-page memorandum commits Octans to invest $4 billion and create 80 jobs in each of five construction phases from 2028 to 2034. OpenAI will pay the equivalent of a 50 percent property tax rate at fixed 2026 millage for 15 years, about $870 million by the authority's estimate. County leaders say the revenue could help eliminate homestead property taxes. The land was already zoned for data centers, so no rezoning vote was needed. "It's a done deal," OpenAI's Aaron McLear told The Current GA.

Residents did not see it that way. Nearly 1,000 people packed an OpenAI open house at the Effingham College & Career Academy in Rincon on July 23. "It stinks," said Larry Holloway, a retired paper mill worker. "That's not how democracy is supposed to work." Commissioner Roger Burdette, who went on the Abilene trip, told the crowd, "I changed my mind," and "You should trust us on this"; he said officials kept quiet because "We didn't want to scare them away." A petition against the project passed 10,000 signatures within days. Blandford Elementary School, with 941 pupils in 2025, is less than a mile from the site, and the industrial park sits in the Floridan aquifer's water use "Red Zone", where withdrawals have been cut to keep out salt water. Jeff Beauvais of One Hundred Miles said: "Obviously a lot of these details and decisions have already been made, and we're playing catch up."

The one formal review so far is advisory.
