The Coastal Regional Commission's 44-page Development of Regional Impact report, released in September, found parts of the site in the 100-year floodplain, wetlands on the tract, and the state-protected hooded pitcherplant growing on it, according to WTOC. It also estimated $20 million a year in local tax revenue at full build-out. In comments attached to the report, the Savannah Riverkeeper asked for binding assurances that the campus will use treated surface water, not groundwater, and that the developer pay for all grid upgrades. One Hundred Miles noted that the filing does not show where the backup diesel generators will go. Savannah will supply Effingham with wholesale water until the county's new surface water plant opens in early 2030. The county commission's consideration of the site plan is postponed at the developer's request while the county drafts stricter conditional-use rules, WTOC reported. The Public Service Commission can review, but not veto, the Georgia Power contract. Camden County has a moratorium on data centers, and Bulloch County to the north has had one since February, extended through December 31.

Sumner County already lives with a hyperscale data center, and that experience drives its fight. Meta's Gallatin campus, first announced in 2020 as "Project Woolhawk," began serving traffic in November 2024 at the Gallatin Industrial Center, about four miles northeast of downtown. It covers 900 acres with four buildings built so far and plans for up to 12, for an expected load of about 300 megawatts at full build-out. Meta puts its investment at $1.5 billion and buys power directly from the Tennessee Valley Authority, matched with solar contracts.

The benefits are real but disputed. The city granted Meta a 20-year PILOT package worth an estimated $19.5 million in tax breaks, and Meta paid an estimated $1.8 million in local taxes in 2025. Mayor Paige Brown now says of the deal: "I probably wouldn't agree to a PILOT." The campus used more than 53 million gallons of water in 2025, about 2 percent of the city's total; Brown says residential sprinklers use more at the summer peak. Brights Lane neighbors describe blasting that shook a house, brown dust during construction, and a low hum at night; Elizabeth Holmes said Facebook sent her a $2,500 check in exchange for a statement that she would not sue.

Councilman Pascal Jouvence proposed a two-year moratorium in June 2026: "We keep trying to push on data centers, but we don't really have any idea of the impact." The Planning Commission recommended a moratorium 5-2, and the council passed it on first reading but cut it to six months, with Brown casting the tie-breaking vote. A second reading is expected next, along with a staff rewrite to tell server closets and edge sites apart from hyperscale campuses.

Coachella has permanently banned data centers, and three more Coachella Valley cities have paused them. The Coachella City Council voted unanimously on August 26, 2026 to prohibit data centers, with an exemption for ordinary server rooms, and the ban took effect 30 days later. That ended Stronghold Power Systems' Coachella Valley Technology Campus, planned on farmland at Fillmore Street and Avenue 52. Palm Springs' 45-day pause, adopted the same night, runs out in mid-October unless the council extends it, and Indio's moratorium runs through October 16.

In February the council had unanimously approved a deal letting a Stronghold subsidiary build a new electric utility for eastern Coachella, with the data center as its anchor customer. Phase 1 was three data halls drawing 270 to 300 megawatts of power on 240 acres, and Phase 2 would add another 300 megawatts, while city documents put Coachella's projected 20-year electric load at just 70 megawatts. After a packed May town hall, on June 4 the council adopted a moratorium and canceled the agreement. "We are the policymakers fixing what we did wrong," Mayor Frank Figueroa said.

Indio adopted its moratorium in June, extended it on July 15 and told staff to draft a permanent ban. Desert Hot Springs has extended its pause for up to two years, and Perris is also moving toward a ban. Cathedral City, Rancho Mirage, Palm Desert, Indian Wells, La Quinta and unincorporated Riverside County have no such limits.

On Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026, two governments in downtown Stockton stepped back from data centers within hours of each other. In the morning the San Joaquin County Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to have staff spend about six months studying large-scale AI and high-intensity data centers in the unincorporated county, covering their effects on agriculture, water, electricity, land use, public safety and county finances. It also asked County Counsel Edward J. Kiernan whether a temporary moratorium could be legally justified in the meantime. The county says there are no data centers and no active applications in unincorporated areas. "Because there are no existing facilities or active applications, that gives us an important opportunity to be proactive," said Supervisor Robert Rickman. Board chair Sonny Dhaliwal said: "We need to put our residents first." The county expects the board to consider an initial 45-day moratorium on approving data center projects in October; ABC10 reported the date as an Oct. 1 meeting.

That afternoon the Stockton City Council voted 7-0 to take data centers out of its 2026-28 Economic Development Action Plan. The draft had listed them under "Revenue Enhancements", alongside auto dealerships and big-box retailers, without naming a developer, a site, a size, or estimates of revenue, jobs, power or water, Stocktonia reported. Nearly 40 people signed up to speak. "This is not the data center item," said Economic Development Director Ricardo Noguera, but Councilmember Mario Enriquez, who made the motion, said that putting the word in the plan "is going to activate people." Vice Mayor Jason Lee said there should be no data centers "developed or approved by staff without public discussion." The vote imposes no moratorium; the city plans community listening sessions starting around mid-November before deciding whether to put data centers back into the plan.

Stockton already has one. Nautilus Data Technologies has run a 6.5-megawatt facility at the Port of Stockton since late 2020. It cools with San Joaquin River water in an intake-and-discharge system through which about 6.5 million gallons a day can pass before being returned to the river, and it employs 10 full-time workers. The city itself pays a Nautilus subsidiary $1,450 a month to back up its public safety network. Nautilus will not disclose how much power it uses, and the port refused Stocktonia's records request. In June 2024 the Central Valley Regional Water Quality Control Board issued a notice of violation after required weekly temperature monitoring was missed at one location. Stocktonia reported that this conflicts with the company's statement that it had been "fully compliant with no violations." In January the environmental group Restore the Delta published a white paper warning that AI infrastructure was taking hold in the Delta in Stockton and Tracy and could strain groundwater and endangered fish such as Delta smelt. What happens next: the October moratorium decision, the six-month county study, and Stockton's listening sessions.
/data-centers/united-states/california/s.unconfirmed: The date Sept. 1 comes from 'Tuesday' in stories dated Sept. 2. The ABC10 story (syndicated on Yahoo) says the board would bring back a 45-day moratorium at an Oct. 1 meeting; the county says only 'in October'. No Tracy data center project was read about in detail. The Restore the Delta figure of 2 million liters of water a day for a typical 100-megawatt data center is the group's estimate and is not used on the page.

paragraphs: Yorkville set out to build its own "data center alley": at one point the Kendall County city west of Chicago was weighing about a dozen proposals across more than 3,000 acres of the Eldamain Corridor. Three have been approved: CyrusOne's 228-acre campus at Eldamain and Faxon roads, Pioneer Development's 1,034-acre Project Cardinal northwest of Route 47 and Galena Road, planned at 1.8 gigawatts of power, and Prologis's 540-acre Project Steel around Galena and Eldamain roads. The council approved Project Cardinal on March 10 after a nearly six-hour meeting, mostly of residents speaking against it, with overflow seating and 165 more people on Zoom.

The approvals came with money and with anger. Cardinal's developers pledged $51 million over four years and Project Steel's developers $40 million, much of it for Yorkville School District 115. Resident Christine Dupler called the deal a "drop in the bucket," and Maria Torres accused the city of being "in it for the money." Cardinal's developers switched to air-cooled closed-loop cooling, cutting projected water use from 350,000 gallons a day to about 42,500. By April, Mayor John Purcell said there was "no more appetite" on the council for further data center proposals.

The fight moved to court. A residents' group, Preserve Our Yorkville & Community LLC, sued the city and the Cardinal and Steel developers, arguing neighbors were not properly notified and that studies of sound, traffic and property values ignored the long construction period. A separate neighbor's lawsuit settled, requiring the section nearest his land to be built last instead of second; the council approved that settlement on July 14. Pioneer has also asked for more time to buy its Cardinal land, and the council extended its deadline from July 1, 2026 to December 31, 2027. If Pioneer does not close by then, the annexation, zoning and $51 million agreement for Project Cardinal all become void.

Grundy County has three data center proposals moving at once, and the biggest is meeting organized resistance. Morris residents who expected to meet Tract, a Colorado "master developer," in person over its 1,000-megawatt campus were offered two Zoom town halls instead, and a petition against it drew more than 100 signatures. According to county records reported by WCSJ, CP Morris Land LLC sold more than 350 acres near U.S. Route 6 and Gun Club Road to ILLCO Grundy County LLC for $51 million on December 19. Tract says the campus would bring $900 million in tax revenue over 20 years and 350 to 400 jobs, by its own projections, and has pledged $10 million toward the city's new water treatment plant.

The opposition is loud and organized. At an Aug. 18 council meeting with no data center item on the agenda, residents used public comment anyway; Jodi Pollack said the city and county board had offered "nothing but a script." Ami Frick, who drove two hours from Grayslake, described construction noise and a $100,000 drop in one neighbor's property value at a Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin data center. The meeting ended with Mayor Chris Brown cutting off comment, and most of the council left through the back door. Brown says the city is finishing a zoning ordinance covering water, noise, setbacks, power generation and decommissioning, to go before council committees in the coming months.

Two more projects are moving elsewhere in the county. In Coal City, Aligned Data Centers wants to build on industrial park land at Reed and Carbon Hill roads; a planned unit development is now before a village review committee after the village held a community meeting in February. North of Minooka, Equinix is building at Ridge and Holt roads; its western U.S. development chief, Guy Danskine, told the Minooka State of the Village address in April that the site "won't use any more water than a typical office building." The Morris zoning ordinance, Coal City's review of the Aligned plan, and the naming of an end user for Tract's site are all still pending.

The one large data center proposed in St. Lucie County, Sentinel Grove Technology Park, also called Project Jarvis, has been withdrawn. It would have covered 1,218 acres of former citrus grove on the east side of Minute Maid Road, north of Orange Avenue (State Road 68) outside Fort Pierce, with up to 15 million square feet of buildings and a first phase of 1,000 megawatts of power.

The county's Planning and Zoning Commission voted 4-2 on October 16, 2025 to recommend against the land-use change it needed. "That's the last agricultural area we have left in St. Lucie County, please don't destroy it," resident Cynthia Adams told the board. Peter Harrison, who owns an 18-acre homestead on Orange Avenue, said, "The numbers are just off the chart." Timberline Real Estate Partners, which filed the request with HJA Design Studios, said it had no tenant.

In February 2026, County Commissioner Cathy Townsend said the applicant had pulled out to wait and see what Florida's data center bill, then before the Legislature, would require. The land is owned by Epic Estates 68 LLC, a Tallahassee firm that bought it for $15 million in July 2024. To revive the plan, the developer would have to submit it to county staff again and ask to bring it to the County Commission.

No new data center has been proposed in Hillsborough County, and commissioners voted 7-0 twice on August 5, 2026 to prepare a ban. One vote ordered a study of water rules, including a possible ban on using county drinking water to cool data centers; the other told the county attorney to draft a moratorium on AI data centers in unincorporated Hillsborough. Because of a 2025 state law passed after hurricanes Debby, Helene and Milton, the moratorium cannot take effect until October 1, 2027, unless a court strikes that law down first.

The county's one working data center is an old one: the Franklin Exchange Building at 655 North Franklin Street in downtown Tampa, a 1966 tower whose 30,400-square-foot data center houses the Tampa Internet Exchange, where networks connect. A new venture, HyscaleIX, formed by H5 Data Centers and the investment firm Novacap, bought it from 365 Data Centers in early 2026.

Development Services Director Adam Gormly said data centers are not an allowed use in the county's land code, and companies that asked were told they are "not eligible for development at this time." Residents at the meeting pointed to about 1,000 acres east of Tampa being marketed as "University Energy Park," a possible data center site; Gormly said no proposal had been filed for it. Commissioner Harry Cohen said the county would "proceed very, very cautiously before we even entertain the idea of allowing anything like this to be built."

The vote came during drought water restrictions. U.S. Rep. Kathy Castor wrote to commissioners on September 10 that she strongly opposes data centers in the county, citing water and electric bills. The staff study and the draft moratorium ordinance come back to the commission for a vote; no date has been set.

QTS is building a data center campus at 2883 Gordon Highway in west Augusta, between the Haynes Station and Captain's Corner subdivisions, where neighbors learned of it only when groundwork began. The plan is six two-story buildings, about 2.2 million square feet, and a $2 billion investment with 160 to 220 permanent jobs, QTS told the Augusta Commission in February 2026. On September 15, 2026, commissioners narrowly adopted, 6-5, citywide rules for any new data center; they do not apply to the QTS campus, which was zoned years earlier.

T5 Data Centers first announced a 200-megawatt campus on the site in January 2022, on what was then an isolated stretch of Gordon Highway, and later dropped out; the homes on either side were built after the first approval. QTS took over an expanded plan, says it will use closed-loop cooling, and groundwork has begun, with buildings promised "into the next few years." Neighbors call the process secretive. "My request is that this commission require clear, enforceable measures for transparency and accountability before we move forward with this project," resident Suzettra Walker told commissioners in June.

The commission paused new data center applications on June 2, 2026, after more than two hours of public comment, and the pause lasted almost three months until the new rules passed. The rules keep data centers out of residential and farm areas, require a public hearing and commission approval in most other zones, set a buffer of at least 500 feet from homes, cap noise at 65 decibels by day and 60 at night, and require closed-loop cooling with no private wells.

Developers are marketing a 150-megawatt data center on a 300-acre industrial campus in northeast Fairfield, between Vanden Road and North Gate Road near the edge of Vacaville. Investor slides from Jones Lang LaSalle and NorthPoint Development call it North Bay Solutions and say a data center is allowed "by right." The land belongs to Canon Partners, whose industrial park plan the Fairfield Planning Commission approved in 2023. No building application has been filed yet; a formal one would need a public hearing.

City spokesperson Bill Way said Canon is studying the cost of bringing in PG&E power. County voters decide Measure E on November 3, 2026. It would tax data centers $5 per square foot of building, about $2 million a year for one big enough for 77 megawatts, but only in unincorporated areas, so it would not reach the Fairfield site. "I want to make sure it is as expensive as possible for them to do that," said board chair Mitch Mashburn as supervisors voted 4-0 on July 28 to put it on the ballot.

Residents also turned out against a pitch for an emergency shelter with a data center at the Solano County Fairgrounds in Vallejo; the fair association pulled the item from its July 15 agenda, saying approval was outside its authority. Rio Vista has warned that Suisun City's proposed annexation of California Forever land would allow data centers by right in some districts.

The data center actually moving through permits in Hartford County is small: a 4-megawatt, fuel-cell-powered computing building on the former Dodge Village car dealership site at 234 Riverside Avenue in Bristol, beside the Pequabuck River. The developer, ReNew Riverside LLC, belongs to Colchester-based ReNew Developers, whose chief executive John Matheson told the Hartford Business Journal in February that Connecticut's only viable data centers are "smaller, lower-impact facilities" that make their own power. The state Siting Council approved the fuel cell in December 2022. Bristol had no zoning category for data centers until its Zoning Commission adopted one in November 2025, opening a path for them in some business and industrial zones. The Inland Wetlands Commission approved the project in April 2026. Mayor Ellen Zoppo-Sassu wrote in April that the building, about 15,000 square feet, would use closed-loop cooling with city water, draw nothing from the river, and install noise monitoring. Matheson said construction was targeted to start in summer 2026, with operations the following year.

Not everyone in Bristol is convinced. A March commentary in The Bristol Edition said the 1.62-acre plan, which it put at 27,000 square feet, would run continuously on a flood-prone riverfront the city is trying to turn into a walkable corridor, with a streetscape rebuild planned as soon as 2027 and the former J.H. Sessions factory becoming housing. It raised questions about storm risk, fuel storage, noise and light. Zoppo-Sassu, who says the project began under the previous administration, argued that it is edge computing rather than a hyperscale campus, and that big data centers "won't be located in Connecticut any time soon" because of the state's power costs. The city's public works director has suggested updating Bristol's noise ordinance to cover the low-frequency hum of generators.

Bigger ideas in the county have stalled on paper. In June 2025 New York-based Atlas Capital Group showed Bloomfield's Planning and Zoning Commission a concept for a two-story data center of about 1 million square feet, with a 127,000-square-foot substation, on a 44.5-acre former tobacco field at 132 Griffin Road North. Commissioners called it "worthy of consideration", but by February 2026 no formal application had been filed. The only applicant to the state's 2021 data center tax incentive program is Bloomfield-based Cigna, for a roughly $380 million upgrade of its Windsor data center. A New Britain proposal pairing a data center with a fuel cell had advanced only on the power side. Gov. Ned Lamont said in February that the state would "slow down new data centers, unless they add more generation as well," and a legislative committee floated repealing some of the tax incentives. What happens next: construction in Bristol if the remaining permits come through, and a formal application in Bloomfield, if Atlas files one.
/data-centers/united-states/connecticut/.unconfirmed: The Bristol building's size differs: 15,000 square feet in the mayor's column, 27,000 in The Bristol Edition commentary. A search preview said the Bristol City Council voted on July 14 to ask the Zoning Commission to lower a size limit in the new data center rules; that was not read and is not used. Whether construction began in summer 2026 was not confirmed. The Bloomfield site's past as a tobacco field is from DCD.

paragraphs: CyrusOne plans a $500 million data center campus on 280 acres of farmland at Thayer and Clark roads in Talkington Township, near Waverly and about 14 miles southwest of Springfield. The County Board approved it 17-10, with one abstention, on April 7, 2026, and neighbors have sued to overturn that vote. Circuit Judge Adam Giganti will hear the county's motion to dismiss the lawsuit on October 9.

The plan is six one-story buildings of 250,000 square feet each, using about 600 megawatts of power when fully built. CyrusOne says its air-cooled system will use water "comparable to a standard office building," that it will pay for all power line upgrades, and that it will hire about 100 permanent workers. The site sits just north of the Double Black Diamond solar farm, and most of the land is tied to Dowson Farms of Divernon.

Supporters point to taxes: the parcel pays about $20,000 to $50,000 a year now, and the county estimates about $6.5 million once the campus is built, close to 70 percent of it to the North Mac School District. CyrusOne sought no local tax breaks but signed a 20-year state tax incentive deal in May. "We have to have work, we have to have jobs," said Josh Summers of the Iron Workers union. Opponents worry about power bills, noise and the planned backup diesel generators.

The April vote came before a packed crowd; some people were escorted out, and public comment was cut off after about a quarter of the more than 60 speakers. On July 6 members of the Caruthers family, who have farmed nearby for close to two centuries, and kennel owner Cathy Bettis sued the county. They argue an industrial project cannot go in a farm district as a conditional use, and that the approval was misdated. As of mid-July, no land had changed hands.

Amazon Web Services has county approval for Project Rise, a $7 billion data center campus of up to nine buildings on 304 acres of NIPSCO land near the R.M. Schahfer Generating Station in Wheatfield. County Commissioners unanimously approved the development agreements on June 15, 2026. No construction start date has been given; AWS is expected to build while NIPSCO finishes a new natural gas plant and a peaker plant at Schahfer that will power the campus.

Part of Amazon's price is water for Wheatfield Township, which relies on private wells: AWS will spend $25 million to expand water service there. It will also pay $98 million up front during construction and more than $23 million a year for 10 years once running, and promises 250 permanent jobs and 425 acres of habitat restoration in the Kankakee River watershed.

Residents objected mainly to water use, power bills and noise. AWS says the campus will be cooled by outside air except on the hottest days, about 2 percent of the year, using about eight million gallons of water a year at full build-out. Under county conditions, AWS pays all new infrastructure costs and takes its cooling water under NIPSCO's existing permit to draw from the Kankakee River, returning it to the river. "If we wait for the state to stuff this on us, we lose the negotiation power up front," Commissioner Craig Standish said.

A developer with no confirmed record of building a data center wants to put four of them on farmland outside Wolcott. Blue Ladder Development's plan calls for four buildings of about 327,600 square feet each, two substations, a warehouse and an office on 322 acres south of U.S. 24, in the county's Mid-America Commerce Park. The company says it will use closed-loop cooling and bring its own power, and has not disclosed a capacity in megawatts.

Lead developer Josh Levine told the Lafayette Journal & Courier on July 1, 2026 that Blue Ladder had not yet bought the land or found a tenant. DCD reported the company may never have completed a data center before: Texas city emails, shared by opponents, show it zoned a parcel in Forney in 2021 but never built there. The plan surfaced after a June 29 open house that White County officials confirmed they were co-hosting with Blue Ladder.

The land is already in court. In August 2025, Wolcott residents Bart and Amy Snyder sued the county commissioners, the redevelopment commission and the landowners to overturn the rezoning of 184 acres near their home, arguing the applications lacked the notarized owner letters and site plan the zoning ordinance requires. A judge heard arguments on their summary-judgment motion on July 27, 2026; no ruling has been published since.

Calvert County has had a six-month moratorium on data center site plans since August 28, 2026, and Amazon has dropped its plan to build next to the Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant in Lusby. The commissioners passed the moratorium on August 18, two weeks after the county announced that Amazon Web Services had withdrawn its application. While the pause runs, into early 2027, the county will not accept or approve data center site plans and will consider new zoning rules.

Amazon had filed plans in May for eight data center buildings, about 2.46 million square feet in all, on mostly forested land owned by Constellation Energy at 1650 Calvert Cliffs Parkway. Voters had already turned on the project: on June 23 all three commissioners who had voted against a pause, Todd Ireland, Mark C. Cox Sr. and Earl F. "Buddy" Hance, lost their Republican primaries. Amazon called its exit a business decision. Melissa Emmal, whose petition for a moratorium passed 10,000 signatures, called it "a welcome development" but noted the company could resubmit.

A second idea came in March, when Natelli Holdings, a Gaithersburg real estate firm, proposed buying a county-owned former Dominion Energy site near Calvert Cliffs State Park for four data center buildings drawing about 300 megawatts of power. The county's data center page now says the government "is not currently pursuing or exploring data center development." Voters pick commissioners in the November 3, 2026 general election.

No new data centers can be permitted in Baltimore County through at least the end of 2027. The County Council voted unanimously on September 22, 2026, to extend the freeze it first passed in February, which would otherwise have ended by January 1, 2027. The Planning Board approved its study of data centers on September 17, and the council now has to review it and decide on permanent rules; council chairman Mike Ertel said he had not yet read it when the extension passed.

The freeze was set off in Woodlawn, where Security Land & Development Co. proposed turning a vacant Social Security Administration building into a 42-acre, 150-megawatt data center. Residents said the mostly minority area already carries more than its share of pollution. "This is a rapidly evolving industry so a moratorium is the most appropriate thing to do," said Councilman Todd Crandell. Some speakers at the September hearing asked for an outright ban, while a union representative asked the council to "end the moratorium early" once rules are ready.

Councilmen Izzy Patoka and David Marks have also proposed repealing the 2024 zoning law that allowed data centers in parts of the county. The only data center operating on the map here is Expedient's small BWI1 center at 11155 Red Run Boulevard in Owings Mills, which lists 800 kilowatts of computer load.

Data centers are not allowed in Peculiar, a Cass County town of about 3,000 south of Kansas City. In October 2024 the Board of Aldermen unanimously removed data centers from the city's light industrial zoning, blocking Diode Ventures' $1.5 billion Harper Road Technology Park. The plan was for up to seven buildings of about 300,000 square feet each on about 500 acres on the west side of Harper Road between 203rd and future 211th streets, next to a new Evergy substation.

Residents organized under the slogan "Don't Dump Data on Peculiar," put up yard signs reading "No Hyperscale Data Centers" and built a Facebook group of about 1,000 members, roughly a sixth of the area's population. Mayor Doug Stark, who had announced the project in January 2024, wrote that aldermen were under pressure from a "boisterous and ill-informed group" trying to "kill" it. Diode said there was no active application in Peculiar and has kept developing other campuses around Kansas City.

A 1,000-megawatt data center that has never been formally proposed to the town has led East Fishkill to close the door for three years. In May 2026 residents learned that New Jersey-based Treetop Companies had asked the New York grid operator to study connecting an AI and cloud computing center on wooded land off Lime Kiln Road, big enough to use as much power as roughly 800,000 homes, with a first phase planned for 2028. On June 25, after a nearly two-hour hearing, the Town Board voted unanimously for a moratorium on large-scale data centers until July 1, 2029.

The town's code does not already permit data centers in industrial zones, and Treetop's related warehouse application had been frozen since September 2024 by a separate town moratorium. The new rule bars permits for any data center "until the completion of federal and state studies" of their power and water use, noise and heat, though it exempts uses under 20 megawatts. "A moratorium gives us time," Supervisor Nicholas D'Alessandro said, noting Treetop had no formal application. Residents' fears centered on water in a town "basically on well water" over aquifers, as Fran Caracappa put it, along with electricity rates, noise and property values.

Treetop's lawyers sent the town a letter objecting to the moratorium, town attorney Thomas Wood said, and the company did not respond to reporters. Some residents asked for a permanent ban, but Wood said state law requires moratoriums to be limited in time. The Times Union counted six other data center proposals in the Hudson Valley, including one at iPark 87, also in East Fishkill.

The state fight runs through Dutchess too. On June 4 the Legislature passed a one-year moratorium on state environmental permits for data centers; in July Governor Kathy Hochul instead issued an executive order pausing state permits for projects of 50 megawatts or more, while the broader bill, reaching centers as small as 20 megawatts, still awaited her decision as of late August. What happens next: her decision on that bill, the task force's recommendations, and whether Treetop challenges the town's pause.

Meta owns 355 acres of farmland in north Davenport and has not said whether it will ever build on them. In May 2024 a Meta-controlled shell company, Vemerald LLC, proposed two data halls and support buildings totaling about 715,000 square feet on land near the Kraft-Heinz plant between Hillandale Road and Enterprise Way. Davenport approved a 60 percent property tax exemption for 20 years, estimated to be worth about $161 million, in return for at least $800 million of investment. The Iowa Economic Development Authority approved Meta's application under the state's High Quality Jobs Program, for 35 jobs. City documents valued the finished facility at $420 million, against $958,000 for the land. Meta paid $21 million for 10 parcels from three owners in July 2024 and March 2025, according to the Quad-City Times' review of county land records. It had said it would break ground in late 2025 and finish by the end of 2027 if it went ahead.

Nothing has been built. "Meta (Vemerald) purchased the land but has not announced any plans to build yet," city spokesperson Denise Hnytka told the Quad-City Times in 2026. The basic numbers are secret. Iowa American Water declined to discuss the project's water use, citing a non-disclosure agreement with Meta, and MidAmerican Energy declined to give its power demand, citing state rules protecting customer information. MidAmerican said it "does not expect the data center, if built, to increase customer rates," because large-load customers now bear the full cost of the infrastructure that serves them. The Quad Cities' existing data centers are small by comparison: Bluebird's in Bettendorf and South Front Networks' in Davenport, whose president said its two sites together use about 20,000 kilowatt-hours a month. Meanwhile Meta said in January 2026 that it expected to spend $115 billion to $135 billion on capital that year, mostly on data centers. What happens next is Meta's call, and it has given no start date.

The Quad-City Times story carries no date in the text read; it refers to Meta's January 2026 spending guidance, so it is from 2026. A WQAD story on the empty land could not be read (access denied). Whether the incentive agreements carry a deadline was not stated in the text read.

paragraphs: No large data center is proposed in Buncombe County, and new ones are on hold. Asheville's City Council unanimously adopted a one-year moratorium on June 23, 2026, running to June 23, 2027, while the city writes rules; Woodfin's council approved its own one-year pause on May 19, 2026. The county itself adopted a moratorium and then, in 2024, restricted where data centers can be built.

Asheville's land-use rules do not even define a data center. Data centers "are forever," Mayor Esther Manheimer said, "so I think we need to take a pause and make sure we put in measures that address all the concerns that we have as a community." City staff cited heavy loads on power and water and noise and heat that bother neighbors; planners will first map where data centers would clash least with homes, then draft standards such as buffers, soundproofing and daily water limits.

Water is tight. Asheville's system can supply about 40 million gallons a day against average demand of about 25 million, and running the treatment plants flat out for a big user would be "akin to continuously redlining a car engine," a city spokesperson said. County planning director Nathan Pennington doubts the mountains suit data centers: "Data centers look for cheap, flat land, two things that are rare in our area." The region's economic development coalition says no developer has approached it and it is not courting any.

Cloverleaf Infrastructure of Houston wants to build Project Bluestem, a data center campus with an on-site gas power plant, on more than 1,000 acres of the former Tailgate Ranch just south of Tonganoxie. It would use up to 1.2 gigawatts, or 1,200 megawatts of power. The county planning commission advanced new data center rules in September, and they go next to the County Commission, which will review Bluestem under them.

On August 5, 2026 commissioners voted 3-2 against extending the county's 90-day moratorium to January 31. Vanessa Reid, Willie Dove and Jeff Culbertson voted no; Mike Stieben and Mike Smith wanted to leave the decision to the three new commissioners who take office in January. "We had a pause to get regulations in place, it didn't happen," said Rebecca Davis of the Tongie Data Center Watch Dog Group. Stieben said the question "comes down to do we think this fits?"

More than 1,000 people came to a county forum at the Leavenworth County Fairgrounds on September 16, most of them opposed; Dove and Smith were absent. Dee Karlskint of Citizens Against Bluestem, who lives two miles from the site, said she fears the "tonal noise" of rooftop cooling equipment. Reid, whose daughter attends a school near the site, said some supporters were afraid to speak publicly. Opponents said they had hired a lawyer and were looking at legal action.

Cloverleaf has not named the tech company behind the project. It says Bluestem will use closed-loop cooling, pay for any power line upgrades and set aside 330 acres for permanent conservation. The project would qualify for Kansas's 20-year, 100 percent sales and use tax exemption.

Marshall sold 270 acres of its Brooks Industrial Park for $1.12 million before most residents knew a data center was coming. On Oct. 30, 2025, the city's Local Development Finance Authority voted unanimously on a purchase agreement with Alterra Development for what it calls the Marshall Technology and Energy Center. Only 112 of the acres are buildable; the rest are split by wetlands beside Stuart Lake and the Brooks Nature Area. The first concept paired a data center with a gas generation plant, about a gigawatt in all. Alterra estimated 300 to 500 skilled jobs and said it would use closed-loop liquid cooling and create developable land through wetland mitigation. Founder James Jarvis promised to keep "the integrity of what Brooks Industrial Park and Brooks Nature Park represented initially." The purchase only opened a due diligence period, which Alterra expected to finish by the third quarter of 2026. Mayor Scott Wolfersberger has said the finance authority did not consider environmental concerns when it approved the sale.

The backlash arrived at a December finance authority meeting where the project was not even on the agenda. "It's our biggest meeting ever," chair Mike Beck said, as residents who said they had heard about the deal only days earlier lined up to speak. "You're treating our Brooks Wetland as if it's wasteland," one said. Several compared it to the Ford BlueOval battery plant, where they had also felt unheard. Wolfersberger argued that the land had been zoned industrial for nearly 60 years and that Marshall needed to replace employers it had lost: "We lost Eaton, we lost State Farm, we've lost Campbell Soup."

On Aug. 3, 2026 the City Council passed a moratorium delaying approval of any data center in the city for 365 days, citing uncertainty about electricity, water and heat discharge. The city plans to use the time to write an ordinance on low-frequency noise and vibration. Wolfersberger said Alterra has since dropped the gas plant, cutting the project's energy use by 60 percent: "It's no longer a hyperscale data center by, you know, most definitions." The noise ordinance is due before the moratorium expires on August 3, 2027, and Alterra would still need a site and project plan review from the city before it could build.

San Francisco-based Prologis spent six months trying to rezone 312 acres of farmland in Washington Township for the 32 Mile Road Technical Campus, a data center site near the Romeo State Airport, then withdrew its application on May 19, 2026. Prologis said it would wait until the township adopts data center rules before reapplying. The township board passed a six-month moratorium on new applications on May 20, in effect from May 23 to November 23, 2026.

Residents packed the first planning commission hearing in December 2025, and the commission postponed a decision three more times while the township rewrote its zoning. Township attorney Robert Seibert warned of a "strong possibility" of lawsuits from developers or neighbors, and a noise consultant urged penalties for the tonal and impulsive sounds a data center can make. Township Engineer Mike Kozak said such a user likely could not connect to the township's water and sewer system.

Three other Macomb County communities have also paused new data centers: Sterling Heights, the Village of Romeo and Armada Township. Township Clerk Audrey Brown, who proposed Washington Township's moratorium, said, "The moratorium will give our community time to put legal safeguards in place."

Hours before the Lansing City Council was due to vote on April 6, 2026, the U.K. company Deep Green withdrew its plan for a downtown data center, and the project died. Deep Green had announced the $120 million project in November 2025 with the Lansing Board of Water & Light. It was a 24-megawatt data center of about 25,000 square feet, with a 16-megawatt natural gas fuel cell plant, on vacant parking lots near South Cedar and East Kalamazoo streets. The pitch was a "different kind of data center": its waste heat would feed the utility's downtown heating loop, which is being converted from steam to hot water. BWL general manager Dick Peffley said that would let the utility eliminate, or shrink by 75 percent, a planned $5 million satellite plant. The company promised to stay within city noise limits, pay for its own power infrastructure, cool with a closed loop using about 500,000 gallons of water a year, "in line with the Wendy's across the street," and donate $120,000 a year to BWL's program for low-income customers facing shutoffs.

The project won a 5-2 planning commission recommendation in March, after an earlier rezoning request had been turned down, but it ran into resistance on the council. Critics raised environmental justice concerns about placing it in a poorer neighborhood. "There's going to be five to ten employees going in there from day to day," said Jerry Norris, arguing that a restaurant or housing would do more for downtown. Council member Trini Pehlivanoglu said the company's promises needed to be "legally binding." Many residents doubted the environmental promises; Michigan Advance noted that the fuel cells would still emit carbon dioxide, at 60 to 70 percent of a conventional gas plant's emissions. Council member Ryan Kost said Deep Green likely withdrew because it lacked the votes for the land sale: "if you can't sell the property, then the entire thing's dead." The company gave no reason, saying only that it would keep working with partners in Michigan.

The lots remain parking for now, and Mayor Andy Schor has asked those who wanted housing there instead to bring forward their own development proposals. Three Ingham County communities have since paused new data centers on their own: Lansing's council adopted a six-month moratorium in July 2026 that runs to January 11, 2027, Meridian Township's runs to November 19, 2026, and East Lansing extended its own moratorium, first passed in March 2026, through March 2027.

Servistar Realties plans what would be New England's largest data center at 199 Servistar Industrial Way in Westfield: 10 three-story buildings, 2.7 million square feet in all, drawing up to 274 megawatts of power when finished. The City Council approved it 9-3 in 2021 with millions of dollars in property tax breaks. In July 2026 the same council voted unanimously for a one-year moratorium on any more data centers, which does not stop Servistar because it already has its approvals.

Water is the main fear. City Councilor Kristen Mello, who led the push for the moratorium, is worried about the Barnes Aquifer that supplies the region: "We cannot keep pretending that our choices do not have consequences." Melissa Glynn, whose family lives about 1,000 feet from the site, said the project "would put me over the edge." Co-owner Paul Corey says the campus will use closed-loop cooling, need at most 10,000 gallons of water a day, and run its backup generators on natural gas, not diesel.

The city-owned Westfield Gas & Electric says Servistar will pay for a dedicated substation, which will take about five years to set up, and that other customers' rates should not rise. Some opponents told The Boston Globe they hope to get the 2021 approvals overturned. In neighboring Holyoke, the City Council voted 9-4 in June 2026 to ban new data centers.

A data center that was never formally proposed set off Lee County's fight over the issue. In November 2025, Inside Climate News reported that Deep River Data, a company with ties to the cryptocurrency industry, had asked state officials about tapping natural gas from an old exploratory well near the Deep River to power an AI data center south of U.S. 421, on the Lee-Chatham line. No application was ever filed, but fears of fracking drew long lines of residents to county and Sanford meetings asking for a moratorium on data centers and fracking.

Commission chairman Kirk Smith called a moratorium "on its face dictatorial." Neighboring Chatham County enacted one in February 2026. In March, Lee's commissioners voted 6-1 to have staff draft moratorium language, but turned instead to permanent standards: minimum setbacks from homes and roads, a ban on metal siding and shipping containers, a 65-decibel noise limit backed by fines of up to $10,000 per failed study, and a ban on any data center tied to fracking. State law bars counties from banning data centers outright.

The first real application came in June. Virginia-based PointOne and local developer Helix Ventures filed for a 300,000-square-foot, 90-megawatt data center on 56 acres off Lower Moncure Road, to be owned and operated by CyrusOne, valued at $900 million with no incentives sought. CyrusOne says its closed-loop cooling system will be filled once, with 250,000 gallons trucked in and "no discharge whatsoever." The project would employ 30 to 40 people; work is planned to begin in fall 2026 with operation by 2028.

A Goodhue County judge has stopped work on Google's data center in Pine Island. On May 22, 2026, District Judge Patrick M. Biren issued a temporary restraining order barring developer Ryan Companies from any construction at Project Skyway, a 482-acre technology park on the edge of the town of about 4,000 people. He also rejected the city's and developer's bid for summary judgment. No hearing or ruling has been reported since.

The Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy sued, arguing the city's 2025 environmental review was "insufficient and illegal" because officials already knew a large Google data center was coming and needed a fuller study of the project's effects. The judge found the group had made "a showing of possible success on the merits." Ryan estimated in court that the delay could cost it $5 million or more.

Pine Island approved a conditional use permit, a zoning approval, in January and, on Feb. 4, a package that abates $36 million in property taxes over up to 28 years while still expecting about $131 million in new property taxes and $27 million more from the developer; Google separately pledged $25 million to Pine Island's schools. Mayor David Friese said the worst case is the legal process "pushing the project out" to 2027.

On August 3, 2026, to applause, five Edgecombe County commissioners voted to bar new data center and crypto-mining approvals in the county until August 3, 2028. Chairman Leonard Wiggins and commissioners Viola Harris, Evelyn Powell, George Thorne and Dewitt Woodley voted yes; two were absent. Residents had delivered petitions with more than 1,000 signatures, and a county advisory group had recommended an outright ban. "Taking 24 months to gather information, monitor changes in state policy, engage the public and strengthen local protections is a responsible and measured approach," said Pamlico-Tar Riverkeeper Katey Zimmerman of Sound Rivers.

The pause followed the collapse of the county's one big proposal. Energy Storage Solutions, run by Dan Shaffer, had sought about 122 acres of county-owned land in the Kingsboro Business Park, between Rocky Mount and Tarboro, describing an eight-phase, $19.2 billion data center and energy storage project powered by on-site gas turbines. County Manager Eric Evans said his team questioned the company's claim of 500 jobs. Separately, Tarboro's town council had denied the company a permit for a related $6.4 billion project, and the company sued. At the commissioners' July meeting, Evans announced ESS had withdrawn; Shaffer said "our investors insisted that we move forward with other projects that we have in friendlier communities," and that ESS expected to settle with Tarboro and drop its suit.

The county's Data Center Advisory Committee, set up after the Kingsboro proposal, has delivered a report whose most-supported recommendation was a ban on hyperscale data centers, and commissioners now have until August 2028 to decide on permanent rules.

Warrenton, west of St. Louis, has given Crusoe Energy Systems everything it needs to build: a unanimous site plan approval in January 2026 and, in April, a tax abatement worth an estimated $1.6 billion over 20 years. The Denver company, named developer in November 2025, plans a 340-acre campus with two 805,000-square-foot data center buildings, a substation and an Ameren switchyard on Interstate 70. The first phase is planned for 2027 and the second for 2028, at $8.3 billion of equipment each; no operator has been announced.

On Jan. 20, after a nearly five-hour meeting, the Board of Aldermen voted 6-0 for the conditional use permit, with noise caps, dimmed lighting and more trees, all of which Crusoe accepted. On April 14 the board voted 4-2 for a 75% abatement of personal property taxes on equipment; Crusoe still pays full real property tax, and the abatement disappears if the promised jobs don't materialize. Mayor Eric Schleuter said Crusoe needed the break to attract one of the "top five" tech companies.

"That's insanity," said resident Jessica Sutton, who objected that the deal was negotiated in closed sessions and that promised community payments were contingent and slow to arrive. A group opposed to the project, Protect Our Way of Life Warren County LLC, has retained a lawyer and is exploring legal options. Crusoe still needs a land disturbance review and several permits before construction can start.

Great Falls' first large data center proposal collapsed before it reached a vote. The Great Falls Development Alliance announced Project Cardinal in June 2025: Atlanta-based Ardent's TAC Data Centers planned a $1 billion to $1.5 billion, 2-million-square-foot campus on 569 acres near the AgriTech park, close to Malmstrom Air Force Base. Ardent asked NorthWestern Energy for 500 to 600 megawatts of power, and by fall 2025 it had withdrawn, saying the timeline for that power did not fit its plans.

"This particular group recognized that the timelines on power from NorthWestern and others just wasn't a good fit," said Jolene Schalper of the development alliance. The land sits outside city limits, so a revived proposal would need annexation and zoning, and the alliance's Brett Doney had cited security next to a nuclear missile base as a factor. The alliance has since formed a data center task force to prepare for another proposal.

On July 28, 2026, the Golden Triangle Resource Council brought Cascade County commissioners a petition of about 250 signatures asking for a county moratorium on data centers until state regulations exist. "We'd prefer to have that done in a public hearing," member Gordon Whirry told commissioners. What happens next: whether commissioners schedule that hearing and act on the moratorium request.

On Sept. 22, 2026, the Montana Supreme Court ordered Butte-Silver Bow not to block a data center ballot measure, keeping alive a question the county had tried to keep off the November ballot. Local Initiative 00-02, from Denise Kelly's group 406 People First, would require two-thirds voter approval in a special election before the city-county can authorize any data center. The fight is over a deadline: election administrator Cynthia Sherman first told organizers they had until Aug. 14 to gather 3,652 valid signatures, then said a 2025 state law actually required them by July 13.

The group turned in 3,850 valid signatures. A district court ruled on Aug. 28 that the earlier statutory deadline applied despite the wrong information from election officials, but the Supreme Court granted an injunction pending appeal, noting the initiative had cleared the signature threshold. "Butte-Silver Bow will follow the Supreme Court's ruling," Chief Executive JP Gallagher said. The measure grew out of Sabey Data Centers' plan for a data center on more than 600 acres at the county's Montana Connections Industrial Park; Sabey backed out in May but is still exploring other sites in southwest Montana.

Gallagher argues the initiative's definition of a data center is so broad it could stop "a new bank from coming into town"; economic developer Evan Barrett called that "pure baloney." Separately, Commissioner Michele Shea asked the county attorney to draft a temporary moratorium, which the county's judiciary committee was scheduled to begin discussing Sept. 9; no result of that discussion has been published. What happens next: the ballot measure goes to voters in November unless the pending appeal changes that first.

Missoula County's pause on data centers began with a small proposal. Idaho-based Krambu had applied to put a data center in the former UFP Edge building at the Bonner Mill Industrial Park, near the Blackfoot River, starting at about 7 megawatts but able to grow to 100. At a June community meeting, a presenter described it as a 29-megawatt facility. On July 6, 2026, the park's general manager, Mike Heisey, withdrew his signature from the application, ending it: "After hearing from the public and understanding what the concerns are, I have decided to withdraw my signature."

More than 100 residents had turned out at a community meeting in Bonner, worried about water, noise, heat and pollution of the Blackfoot, and warning a small facility could open the door to larger ones. Three days after Krambu withdrew, on July 9, commissioners unanimously adopted a one-year moratorium on new data centers outside Missoula city limits, after 30 public commenters all spoke in favor. Planning director Karen Hughes said the county's 2021 zoning rules do not cover water, air quality, heat or the "24/7 low-frequency noise" of modern data centers.

County attorney John Hart said the county cannot ban data centers permanently, and the pause can be extended once more. A study to justify the moratorium is due within 30 days, and new regulations are expected before it expires on July 8, 2027. Commissioner Josh Slotnick said the 2021 rules were written when "a data center meant something very different than what it means right now."

Amazon Web Services opened a data center in Clinton on June 9, 2026, in the former Milwaukee Tool building at 1001 Industrial Park Drive. It is AWS's fourth data center in Mississippi, and local leaders said it would bring more than 100 technology jobs. AWS's Roger Wehner said the site will not use water for cooling.

The project moved fast and, at first, without a name. Talks began in July 2025, and on January 15, 2026 the Clinton Board of Aldermen and the Hinds County Board of Supervisors, at special meetings, approved a deal with an unnamed company to pay a yearly fee instead of normal property taxes. WLBT later found a deed showing the 99-acre site went to Amazon Data Services on February 13. Mayor Will Purdie called the $750 million project the "largest economic development project in the history of the city and Hinds County."

Since then, Clinton has changed its zoning so that any future data center needs a conditional use permit, with a Planning Commission hearing before the Board of Aldermen votes. A separate ordinance setting buffers, screening and setbacks for data centers was drafted in July 2026 but had not yet gone to the board for a vote.

Callaway County has no planning and zoning outside its towns, so its commissioners are negotiating with a $4.5 billion data center on the only terms they have: taxes and contracts. Denver-based Crusoe plans a hyperscale campus on about 200 acres of private farmland in the northwest Kingdom City area. It would be the largest private investment in county history, officials say. The location has not been disclosed, which officials attribute to the seller's privacy. At a July 14, 2026 open house in Kingdom City, attended by hundreds, Crusoe showed two buildings of about 800,000 square feet each, promised 70 full-time jobs averaging $89,700, more than 2,000 construction jobs, over $100 million a year in real estate taxes and $15 million for emergency services and health care facilities. It said construction could start anywhere from fall 2026 to summer 2028. The plan keeps shifting: it began as one building, and by late July Commissioner Christopher Scott said Crusoe might build three smaller ones. Early descriptions spoke of closed-loop cooling with a glycol mix. At the open house Crusoe said it would use 100 percent air cooling and no water for servers. It did not provide a power figure.

"It's not an absolute done deal," Scott told the Fulton Rotary Club; no land had been bought and no water or power agreement signed. Presiding Commissioner Gary Jungermann said Callaway Electric Cooperative has told the county it has no additional power to offer, and Scott said that shortage "kind of imposes its own moratorium" on any second data center. The county plans an 80 percent abatement on personal property such as servers under a Chapter 100 deal, with no break on real estate, and hopes to write noise limits or job guarantees into it, as other counties have. Residents' worries were water, power bills, noise and lost farmland. Auxvasse resident Cathy Vogelweide warned that "the land going under this will never be farmed again." Officials point to Missouri's 2025 Senate Bill 4, which makes large-load customers pay the costs of their electricity and connections. What happens next: the land purchase, agreements with Callaway Electric and the Callaway 2 Water District, and the commission's vote on the abatement.
