A search preview gave the campus as 500 megawatts; Crusoe did not give the News Tribune a power figure, and the page uses none. Whether the abatement has been voted on was not found.

paragraphs: A 3-3 tie on the Columbia City Council in November 2025 stopped a rezoning that residents feared would bring a data center. Landowner Gordon Arbuckle wanted 63 acres of farmland at 3815 Hinkson Creek Road, northeast of U.S. 63 and Paris Road, rezoned from agriculture to industrial for what he called a technology hub. His developer said a data center would count as light industry there. The city's Planning and Zoning Commission had recommended the rezoning 7-2 in October. At the council meeting, residents in the packed chamber wore stickers reading "Save Farmland: No Data Center." Isaac Ellis, a farmer who lives nearby, said: "There's a commodity that is being sold, bought and eaten on that farm right now, and we have no clue what will come after." With Sixth Ward council member Betsy Peters absent, the rezoning failed on the tie.

Columbia then moved to write rules before anyone else came. The council unanimously adopted a definition of a data center, and after an 8-0 planning commission vote, a requirement that any new one get a conditional use permit. It also voted 6-0 to have staff bring forward a six-month pause on processing data center applications while standards are finished. "They do not have the right to take our own goods, wreck our natural resources and leave us to pick up the tab," said Fourth Ward council member Nick Foster, citing complaints about AI data centers in Memphis. The planning commission has been drafting location criteria: distance from schools, parks, trails and homes, road access, and noise, light and vibration buffers. It plans to take up decommissioning, water use and electric demand next. "If we don't do this, we would have no guidelines for a data center and that would put us in a position where we are trying to play catch-up," said commission chair Sharon Jones. What happens next: the commission's remaining standards, then draft regulations released for public comment, including through the city's BeHeard site.
/data-centers/united-states/missouri/boo.unconfirmed: The date of the council's data center definition and pause vote is not in the text read; a search preview placed it in April 2026. The KOMU planning commission story is undated in the text read. Whether the six-month pause was formally adopted, and whether Boone County government outside Columbia has acted, were not found. The Hinkson Creek Road tract's later status was not found.

paragraphs: Data centers cannot be built on Nobles County farmland after the County Board voted 3-2 on April 21, 2026 to reject a zoning change that would have allowed them. The vote stopped Geronimo Power's $4 billion plan for a data center complex on about 950 acres just east of Reading and north of Worthington, in Elk Township. Geronimo said it would consider other options, "including some other communities that have expressed interest."

About 300 people packed the planning commission hearing on April 8, where 19 people spoke for the project, including three Geronimo representatives and one from Nobles Cooperative Electric, and 18 spoke against. The commission voted to keep data centers out of the agricultural preservation district, with only Brent Feikema dissenting. That district covers 70 to 80 percent of the county; farming is "our number one industry," County Administrator Bruce Heitkamp said. County scoping documents estimated the project would have paid about $7 million a year in taxes.

At the board vote, Commissioners Chris Dybevick and Robert Demuth wanted staff to keep working on other ordinance options. "I don't believe moving this to another site within the county is going to alleviate any of the issues I hear from constituents," Commissioner Gene Metz said. Geronimo president Blake Nixon told MPR News: "if the community doesn't want it, we're not going to force it on the community."

Anne Arundel County has paused new data centers for 15 months. The County Council voted unanimously on September 21, 2026, to turn Nathan Volke's proposed ban, Bill 63-26, into a moratorium expiring in January 2028. Data centers already built or under development can keep going and may expand onto adjacent lots. A study group, with a chair and seven members named by the council and four named by the county executive, will recommend permanent rules, and council member Julie Hummer said the pause would lift early if it reports early.

The ban was softened largely because of Fort Meade, the state's largest employer, whose backers warned it would hurt defense contractors. Microsoft also asked for the exception: it has been building a campus at the Annapolis Junction Business Park since 2020, and its government affairs director, Kaitlin Monaghan, said a ban would be "devastating to the remaining phases of this project." Residents backed a pause over power and water. "What concerns me isn't only the data centers themselves, but everything that comes with them," said Brenda Cintron of Hanover.

The one site mapped here is Sandy Farms at 7665 Sandy Farm Road in Severn, a data center building developed by Oppidan for the investor Harrison Street starting in 2020. It is fully leased to a single user, and GI Partners bought it in early 2026.

On the day in August 2026 that Yadkin County commissioners voted 5-0 for a two-year moratorium on data centers, a data center company announced it was buying 120 acres in Yadkinville that the moratorium does not reach. WhiteFiber, operating through its subsidiary Enovum Data Centers, agreed to pay $60 million for two Unifi industrial properties with about 500,000 square feet of warehouse space. It plans to retrofit them into campuses called NC-2 and NC-3, with at least 60 megawatts of initial capacity, potentially about 200 megawatts over time, and first service targeted for the third quarter of 2027. The sites are about 55 miles from WhiteFiber's NC-1 campus in Madison, in Rockingham County, another former Unifi plant. County Manager Michael Silverman said the moratorium covers only unincorporated areas, not towns. Yadkinville's town manager, Mike Koser, noted that because the Unifi properties are already zoned industrial, there is no zoning hurdle to a data center there.

The moratorium grew from a 12-month proposal to two years on a motion by Commissioner Cliff Collins, after more than an hour of public comment against data centers from more than 20 speakers. They were worried about water for farms, lost farmland, noise and rural character. "My family has been farming since the 1800s," said Janet Robbins. "We need our farmers, and we don't need to use our land for data centers." Ashley Bell, a physician assistant running for the 10th Congressional District, warned about low-frequency hum. One resident, Dean Swaim, argued for a shorter, six-month pause and for taxing data centers to relieve property owners, since "Yadkin County has always gotten the crumbs from the counties around them." Local leaders said they were as surprised by the same-day announcement as anyone. In September WhiteFiber's Madison operations manager, Jonathan Collins, told the Yadkinville Town Board that the company cools with outside air and runs generators only for backup. Residents pressed him on what happens when the technology dates and a retrofitted building is abandoned; "I think this could be a testing ground where we can't stop this," said Worth Shover of Boonville.
unconfirmed: The fourth-quarter 2026 closing date is from a search summary of WhiteFiber's announcement; the Elkin Tribune gives the $60 million price but the closing sentence was cut off in the text read. The exact date of the commissioners' meeting ('Monday') was not given in the text read; WFDD's story is dated Aug. 19, 2026. Water and power sources for NC-2 and NC-3 were not reported.
Review (lane v): the closing sentence giving WhiteFiber's expected fourth-quarter 2026 closing was cut because, as noted above, it came from a search summary.

paragraphs: Rockingham County's data center occupies a former Unifi yarn plant on Island Drive in Madison, which closed in 2025 after more than 30 years as production moved to Yadkinville and Central America. Enovum Data Centers, a Bit Digital company, paid $45 million for the nearly million-square-foot plant on about 95 acres, and its sister company WhiteFiber is converting it into an AI data center campus called NC-1. WhiteFiber says it has 99 megawatts secured from Duke Energy and could grow to 200 megawatts, with an eventual investment of more than $1 billion and at least 60 jobs.

Local officials welcomed it from the start. "Their planned investment of over $1 billion will be a tremendous boost to the county and town of Madison," said Kevin Berger, chairman of the county Board of Commissioners. In December 2025, WhiteFiber signed a 10-year, roughly $865 million deal with London-based Nscale for 40 megawatts of capacity at Madison, with Nscale set to start paying for the power in stages beginning in April 2026.

WhiteFiber's operations manager, Jonathan Collins, told a neighboring Yadkinville town board meeting in September 2026 that the company buys already-industrial-zoned buildings to reach the market faster, runs emergency generators "for one hour, once a week," and cools with outside air in a closed loop rather than large volumes of water. Residents at that meeting asked what happens to the retrofitted plant when the technology becomes obsolete, and what chemicals are used in the cooling loop.
WhiteFiber opened the Madison campus to Rockingham County residents for a town hall on September 19, 2026.

New Orleans shut the door on data centers in January 2026 before the first one had formally applied. MS Solar Grid Data, a company founded in 2025 that markets solar-powered data centers under the name Data One Eastern Rise, sent letters in November 2025 announcing plans for a two-phase data center on vacant land at 10251 I-10 W Service Road and 10200 Plainfield Drive, near Interstate 10 and Read Boulevard in New Orleans East. It sought a rezoning from single-family residential to auto-oriented commercial, because the city code had no category for data centers. Residents objected over water, the strain on the Entergy grid and environmental harm. The Alliance for Affordable Energy said the project would "perpetuate environmental racism" in a predominantly African American and Vietnamese American community long burdened by industry. A Change.org petition drew more than 200 signatures.

At a special meeting in late January, the City Council passed two motions. One tells the City Planning Commission to define data centers in the zoning ordinance and set standards for them. The other creates an interim zoning district pausing data center licenses and approvals citywide for at least a year. District E council member Jason Hughes, who represents New Orleans East, told residents "we have heard you loud and clear." "We are not a sprawling 700 mile parish. We are New Orleans," Council President JP Morrell said. Former mayoral candidate Frank Scurlock backed the project for the tax revenue. MS Solar Grid Data's chief executive, James Ramsey, who also runs JC Property Management, said the council had announced "that we're a city that don't know what the future is" and that the center would have brought 30 to 40 permanent jobs. He said he would look to another parish and had no new plans for the Read Boulevard site. The City Planning Commission must next write the zoning standards for data centers, and the council could extend the pause when it expires in January 2027.

A data center cannot legally be built in unincorporated Calcasieu Parish right now, because the parish has no ordinance allowing one, the first obstacle facing a St. Louis developer eyeing wooded land near Moss Bluff. Azimuth Renewables confirmed in September 2026 that it holds an April option on about 1,100 acres north of Coffey Road, between Paul White and North Perkins Ferry roads, roughly eight miles north of Lake Charles. "We are in the evaluation stage for this site and are still determining whether or not a project could work at this location," said company president David Bunge.

The company says any buildings would sit on a fraction of the land, that its wooded, largely flood-zone edges would buffer noise and views, and that the project would pay for its own infrastructure upgrades. Parish spokesman Joseph Booth said there is no land-use ordinance allowing data centers in unincorporated areas and "no proposed timeline" for one, which makes a data center effectively barred there for now.

Moss Bluff residents were already fighting a neighboring proposal: a 4,700-acre solar farm with up to 2.5 million panels on the site next door, from California-based Orion Renewable Energy Group. State Rep. Brett Geymann said the data center news "has elevated the opposition" to the solar farm, warning that approving it "would almost certainly open a gateway for the data center." He and three other state legislators asked the planning and zoning board to deny the farm's zoning variance, and Geymann said Moss Bluff has no heavy commercial or industrial zoning at all.

Police Juror Darby Quinn, whose property borders the 1,100 acres, said he opposes "any industrial-sized development in Ward 1," and Beauregard Electric general manager Mike Viator, speaking as a resident, said he worried about property values. The solar farm's zoning variance could come up for a vote as early as November 2026; a date has not been set, and Azimuth has not said whether it will move ahead with the data center site.

The one data center proposed in Onondaga County is Ranalli Super DC's 300-megawatt plan for a 124-acre industrial site at Hencle Boulevard and Oswego Road in Lysander, where the developer already has approval for a warehouse. No formal application has been filed with the town. Lysander's six-month moratorium, adopted unanimously on May 7, 2026, runs to November 7, 2026, and any application would go to the town planning board.

More than 350 residents came to the May 7 meeting to oppose the plan, and a petition against it passed 1,500 signatures, citing wildlife, air and water, home values and the risk that National Grid passes upgrade costs on to customers. Johanna Bock of Citizens for Lysander worries about who would answer for problems if a facility were sold to a shell company: "So we as a community could have issues and we wouldn't have anywhere to go to." Supervisor Kevin Rode said the state's one-year pause on permits for big data centers covers the site because nothing had been filed before it began.

The county cannot ban or pause data centers itself, so towns are acting on their own. By June 2026 DeWitt, Lysander, Manlius, Salina and Van Buren had moratoriums and Skaneateles had banned data centers outright, county Planning Director Troy Waffner told legislators; Clay adopted a one-year moratorium on June 29, 2026, though no data center has been proposed there. The county is paying up to $500,000 for a neutral consultant's study to help towns decide. "This is not a pro-data center study," Waffner said.

Amherst's zoning board took less than 24 hours to reject a data center for the old Nordson campus, and the developer helped make the case against himself. Illinois-based Cervenka Development Partners asked on July 14, 2026 for a use variance to convert three buildings at 100, 200 and 300 Nordson Drive, about 240,000 square feet of office, warehouse and lab space on the Nordson Corporation campus, into a data center of about 45 megawatts. Nordson, founded in Amherst in 1954, moved its manufacturing to South Carolina in late 2024 and is selling the northern buildings, which have their own substation. Amherst's code does not mention data centers, so the city requires a variance for one. Mayor Mark Costilow said he never expected a data center proposal in a city of about 13,000. The application promised "minimal water and sewer demand" and closed-loop cooling.

On July 29 more than 100 people came to City Hall, so many that most were turned away at the door and listened on their phones outside. "We're a quiet little community. This is not good for the residents," said Christine Burman. An attorney for a group of homeowners, Gerald Phillips, argued the application was invalid because Cervenka did not own the property. Tom Cervenka argued the buildings were so specialized that another manufacturer would be hard to find, then conceded: "Am I gonna tell you that there is no other user that can use these buildings? No." In its written decision the next day, the board said he had undermined his own case. "The board has spoken. The people have spoken," Costilow said, adding that the city would defend the decision in court. Cervenka's deadline to appeal to Lorain County Common Pleas Court passed August 29; no result has been published. It is up to Amherst City Council whether to consider a moratorium, which Costilow thinks is unnecessary.

Asked in September 2026 whether a proposed data center in Tooele Valley was dead, Utah Inland Port Authority director Ben Hart said "dead is a very strong word," but "I don't consider it alive right now, that's for sure." The project area is the port authority's 585 acres near Burmester Road and Interstate 80, near the south shore of the Great Salt Lake. Its plan lists data centers among the industries that could get incentives, and the wider project was reported to include a 500-megawatt data center and a truck stop.

Separately, the Army has conditionally picked CyrusOne to build a data center on about 1,200 acres of the Dugway Proving Ground, further south in the county; the Skull Valley Band of Goshute Indians has opposed it over groundwater concerns.

Emails obtained by the residents' group TooeleCARES show developer Chuck Akerlow of Zenith Development pressing county officials behind the scenes on the Tooele Valley project. In September 2025 he wrote that he had committed to bring a 24-inch high-pressure gas line able to produce 140 megawatts, that he was under nondisclosure agreements with "companies you will recognize," and that he had a letter of intent with a nuclear power company.

In July 2026 he complained that the county's draft data center ordinance discriminated against technology companies, and he floated annexing into Grantsville. Akerlow and a Zenith partner sit on the Interstate Technology Park Public Infrastructure District that could finance infrastructure for the project, and Akerlow has said the project needs port authority financing to work.

Residents organized. At an Aug. 12 hearing the county planning commission heard opposition to a new data center ordinance and to plats for a truck stop and fast-food outlet in the project area, and tabled both, the plats pending a third-party traffic study. In September TooeleCARES delivered a letter signed by more than 1,100 people asking the port authority not to finance the district. "We all live by the same dying (Great Salt) Lake, and our wells are already struggling," resident Amy Lawson told the board.

Hart promised nothing would come to his board without "a very clear green light" from the community: "Tooele Valley (and) Tooele County are signaling they are not OK with it." The county has paused data center applications until its ordinance goes to the planning commission, expected in October, and the County Council, expected in November. Under the state's new HB507, from May 2027 local incentives for large-load data centers will require a state-overseen regionally significant development zone.

La Pine's City Council rejected a proposed 20-megawatt data center on May 27, 2026, ending months of public opposition. Bitcoin miner Boxminer had proposed the project on county-owned industrial land on Reed Road, promising up to 80 jobs and closed-loop cooling that neither consumes nor discharges water. On March 25 the council had voted, in what it called a non-binding step, to start a purchase-and-sale process for the site; Deschutes County, which owns the land, would also have had to agree.

Nearly 100 people packed a May 13 meeting where the data center was not even on the agenda; public comment ran nearly three hours, almost all of it opposed. "We'll be pulling from the same stressed aquifer," said resident Zachary Kraus. A petition drew about 750 signatures. On May 27 the council voted unanimously to reject the land sale after City Manager Geoff Wullschlager raised questions about the developer's job and revenue estimates. "We do listen to you because we live here as well," Council President Cathi VanDamme told the crowd.

The Homer City Energy Campus would turn the site of a former coal-burning power plant in Homer City, about 50 miles east of Pittsburgh, into a 3,200-acre gas-fired campus generating its own power for data centers. Homer City Redevelopment plans about 4.4 gigawatts from natural gas turbines, with power to start in 2027 and an initial investment of about $10 billion. Amazon Web Services has confirmed it is discussing a data center there with Homer City Redevelopment, but says it has no definitive agreement.

Pennsylvania's Department of Environmental Protection issued the plant's air quality permit in 157 days, well ahead of its own 285-day estimate, after more than 500 public comments. The Clean Air Council's executive director, Alex Bomstein, called the permit "illegal" and said "the speed with which DEP rushed this permit through, especially given the magnitude of the pollution and the number of people who are going to die because of it, is troubling." The developer says the new turbines will cut emissions by up to 65 percent compared with the old coal plant, which the council disputes given the scale of the new campus.
What happens next is delivery of the turbines and a tenant agreement. Neither has a public date yet.

A rezoning for data centers on the edge of a Civil War battlefield has been stuck in court for three years. On April 25, 2023, the Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 to rezone about 2,600 acres at Routes 3 and 20 near Locust Grove, next to the Wilderness Battlefield and across from Lake of the Woods, for Wilderness Crossing. The developer, KEG Associates III, plans 26 land bays with up to 5,000 homes, commercial space and 732 acres of industrial use, including data centers. It was the largest rezoning in county history. Nondisclosure agreements between Amazon Web Services and the supervisors initially kept residents from knowing which company was behind the data center portion. A Freedom of Information suit by the Piedmont Environmental Council later showed Amazon had been involved since at least April 2022, according to the American Battlefield Trust. The site also holds unreclaimed gold mines, including the Vaucluse mine, with contaminants such as mercury, arsenic and lead.

In May 2023 the American Battlefield Trust, Central Virginia Battlefields Trust, Friends of Wilderness Battlefield and several residents sued. They argue the plan was approved the same evening it first appeared on the supervisors' agenda, differed from what the Planning Commission had reviewed, and used a "secretive and unlawful zoning process". The county called the suit "a desperate attempt to substitute the opinions of a few landowners for the legislative will of the board," and said 40 percent of the land would stay green space. After a hearing before Judge David B. Franzén, the Orange County Circuit Court ruled on Sept. 16, 2025 that four of the seven counts could proceed to trial; the lawsuit has so far halted construction. The president of the Lake of the Woods homeowners' association, whose gated community houses about 10,000 people, wrote that the project's visual, noise and environmental impacts would be severe. In 2024 the National Trust for Historic Preservation put the Wilderness on its list of the 11 most endangered historic places because of the development. What happens next: the Virginia Mercury reported in April 2026 that the county had asked the circuit judge to send the case to the appeals court before any trial; no trial date has been set.
/data-centers/united-states/virginia/ora.unconfirmed: A search preview said Orange County began in January 2026 to remove data centers as a by-right use in all zoning districts, with a board hearing set for April 14, 2026; no article confirming that was read. The data center square footage and power at Wilderness Crossing were not in the text read. The ruling date comes from the American Battlefield Trust, a party to the suit. Whether the county's request to take the case to the appeals court was granted was not found.

paragraphs: Sioux Falls could get its first large data center on former Xcel Energy land between the city and Brandon. Los Angeles-based Gemini Capital bought about 160 acres from Xcel and plans a 500-megawatt Sioux Falls Technology Park south of East Rice Street, next to Xcel's Split Rock Substation. The city council annexed the land in October 2025 and rezoned 145.6 acres to light industrial in January 2026. Planning director Jeff Eckhoff said in spring 2026 the project still needed more approvals and could be denied; no later update on its status has been published.

Residents' objections have centered on power and water. One resident told the council, "This one facility is projected to more than double our entire city's energy consumption." The zoning requires any data center to sit at least 200 feet from the property line, and the city says Gemini may use city water only for domestic purposes, not cooling. Kyle Peters of A1 Development Solutions, which represents Gemini, said "the goal is to get to 500 megawatts of power," but would not name an investment figure or commit to a cooling system.

Xcel says its data center contracts require developers to pay their own costs and early exit fees, but The Dakota Scout reported that nothing in state law requires residential customers to be protected from those costs. Gemini's website says a fully built 500-megawatt campus with closed-loop cooling would use about as much water as two commercial car washes.

Mayes County has hosted a Google data center for 15 years, at the MidAmerica Industrial Park near Pryor. Google opened its first building there in 2011, added a second in 2012, and by 2019 had invested more than $3 billion and employed over 400 people at what state officials called its second-largest data center in the world. In August 2025 Oklahoma announced a further $9 billion of Google investment over two years, including expansion at Pryor and a new campus in Stillwater; Google now says it has put more than $15 billion into the state.

The clearest effect has been on the tax base: the Pryor school district's assessed valuation rose 168 percent between 2011 and 2015, to $325.6 million, and the county's rose 82 percent, to $498.4 million, according to the state Commerce Department. Superintendent Lisa Muller said the district's assessed value has grown from about $80 million to $1 billion over roughly 20 years, funding a new high school and an approved middle school and stadium. Rents rose and housing tightened as workers arrived, which Pryor Information Publication editor Tim Lawson called "more shame on Pryor, not shame on Google."

Whether a $15 billion data center campus on an old dynamite plant in Lawrence County can go ahead may turn on a box of plans and three returned checks. Stonebridge of Bethesda, Maryland, through its affiliate S.S. Penn LLC, wants to build 16 data center buildings and a substation on the 569-acre former Powder Mill Works at 3478 Howard Drive and McClelland Avenue, off Route 551, straddling North Beaver and Mahoning townships next to the Hickory Run Energy power plant. American Cyanamid made powders there, including nitroglycerine explosives and dynamite, until 1972, so the land needs remediation first. Stonebridge says Penn Power would supply electricity, promises 3,000 to 4,000 jobs over about six years of building, and may use treated wastewater from the nearby Mahoning sewer plant. Its computing capacity has not been disclosed. DatacenterDynamics describes Stonebridge as a residential and commercial developer that has recently moved into data centers.

Both townships were writing data center rules as the plans arrived. Stonebridge delivered its preliminary plans on June 2, 2026; the zoning officer rejected them because the fee checks were wrong, and a Lawrence County escrow check went back and forth until June 15. Mahoning adopted stricter rules on June 24, with lower noise limits and a conditional-use hearing, after first passing rules in April; North Beaver also tightened noise limits and setbacks. On July 1 S.S. Penn sued both townships in the Lawrence County Court of Common Pleas, arguing its application predates the stricter rules. Stonebridge's lawyer, Shawn Gallagher, told a hearing that under the stricter rules the company might not have a project, WKBN reported. The townships' solicitor, Lou Perrotta, argues that under the pending-ordinance doctrine a developer must comply with rules already reviewed and advertised, even if not yet adopted. Residents gathered 170 signatures against the scheme by mid-July, and an informal citizens' group asked about Stonebridge's record of building large data centers elsewhere. What happens next: the court's ruling on which rules apply, and the Mahoning Township zoning hearing board's decision on Stonebridge's appeal.

San Angelo has two large data center projects side by side, and only one of them is under the city's control. The first is Skybox's campus, with its partner Emergent, on about 350 acres of city-owned land northeast of town near U.S. 67 North and City Farm Road. The city council voted 6-0 in May 2025 to negotiate the sale, at about $50,000 an acre or roughly $17.4 million, and took up a zone change in January 2026.

Skybox plans six four-story buildings of 248,000 square feet each, a 600-megawatt campus drawing on spare capacity at the Red Creek substation, of which the city uses only about 10 percent. It would qualify for the state's automatic 6.25 percent sales tax exemption on data center equipment, while the city negotiates a Chapter 380 agreement rather than a traditional property tax abatement. The project has drawn organized local opposition.

The second is Cipher Digital's 1,000-megawatt Colchis site next door, in the unincorporated county. Cipher says it has a direct-connect agreement with American Electric Power and expects Colchis to be included in "Batch Zero," the framework ERCOT's board approved in June 2026 for studying large power connections together rather than one at a time. A state official said it was unclear whether Red Creek could reliably power both projects, and Skybox risks missing its 2028 target if it cannot.

Because Colchis sits outside city limits, San Angelo has no power to regulate its water use or build-out. Tom Green County commissioners have been cautious about regulating data centers, which observers link to a lawsuit against Jefferson County after it tried to restrict them. The next milestone is ERCOT's list of Batch Zero projects, due to show which project gets power first.

A 180-megawatt data center is planned inside Strasburg's industrial park, on land zoned industrial where, according to the town, the "data center use is by-right." Takanock's Project Tallmadge would sit on about 80 to 87 acres near Interstate 81's Exit 296 and the Mercury Paper plant. Takanock, founded in 2023 by Kenneth Davies, formerly head of Google Energy and later of Microsoft's global renewable strategy, and funded by DigitalBridge, says it will bring its own power: 400 megawatts of on-site natural gas generation, with closed-loop cooling. It expects remaining permits by the third quarter of 2027 and construction to start then; the county says the work could run from late 2027 to around 2030. Takanock promises "hundreds of construction jobs" and more tax revenue for the town. Opposition dates from March 2025, when the project first surfaced, over air quality, noise, pollution, water and power; an online petition drew 73 signatures.

On June 15, 2026, residents packed Strasburg High School for a public forum moderated by Mayor Brandy Hawkins Boies, who stressed it was not a council meeting or a vote. An 11-person panel worked through 56 submitted questions on emissions, public health, noise, fire response and oversight. It included the National Parks Conservation Association, the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality, Friends of the North Fork of the Shenandoah River and the Alliance for the Shenandoah Valley, alongside a geologist, the engineering firm Bowman Consulting and Takanock. Boies said she hoped people left understanding "how we got here and what our process is moving forward." What happens next: the remaining permits, which Takanock expects to have by the third quarter of 2027, with construction to follow.
/data-centers/united-states/virginia/she.unconfirmed: The site is given as 87 acres (DCD) and 80 acres (WHSV). The forum date comes from WHSV's 'Monday night' in a June 16 story. The town's own project pages could not be read. The investment total was seen only in a search summary ($4.5 billion) and is not used.

paragraphs: Appomattox County supervisors voted in September 2026 on a $3 billion data center they had no power to stop. In December 2024 the county Economic Development Authority agreed to sell Avaio Digital a 452-acre site in the county industrial park, off U.S. 460 and Virginia 26 just north of the town of Appomattox, for about $4.5 million. The parcel had sat vacant since the county bought the park about 25 years ago. Because data centers were allowed by right there, the project needed no special permit, public hearing or board approval. Avaio calls it "Project Hercules" and plans six data centers drawing 300 megawatts from Central Virginia Electric Cooperative and Dominion Energy, energized in 2027; it has several data centers in development but none operating. EDA chairman Garet Bosiger said the county of about 15,000 had never recovered from Thomasville Furniture's closure in 2011: "Appomattox needed a shot in the arm."

Residents heard about it mostly after the fact. The EDA's first public information session, in March 2026, came more than a year after the announcement; nearly 100 people attended, and several said the format left no room to speak. Dennis Bradner, who lives near the site, said the animosity was "because nobody explained anything." Opponents raised electricity costs, water, noise and air pollution. On Sept. 21 the supervisors approved a performance agreement giving Avaio annual payments based on the tax revenue the project generates, with Supervisor Trevor Hipps the only vote against. Chairman John Hinkle said the board had no authority to stop the project; Supervisor Nathan Simpson, credited with making the first introductions, pointed to project job postings paying $150,000 and $210,000. What happens next: the state Department of Environmental Quality's decision on an air permit for the site's backup generators, due by mid-December after a public comment period that opened Sept. 11. In the region, Campbell and Amherst counties and Lynchburg have changed their zoning to require more approvals for data centers, the News & Advance reported.

Charles City County, a rural county about 20 miles east of Richmond that had to borrow $5 million in 2024 to avoid running out of cash, was offered a way out by a data center, and the offer collapsed under local opposition. Diode Ventures, a subsidiary of Kansas City engineering firm Black & Veatch, asked in 2025 to rezone about 515 acres of woods in the county's northwest corner, bordered by Charles City, CC and Roxbury roads, from agricultural to light industrial for the Roxbury Technology Park. Diode did not say how many buildings or how much power, but a presentation to supervisors suggested the campus could bring as much as $52 million in real estate taxes and $88 million in business personal property taxes over 20 years. The county's real estate tax collections are under $7 million a year. Diode promised 800 to 1,200 construction jobs and 50 to 100 permanent ones, and also sought approval of a centralized wastewater facility. A county staff report called digital commerce "the next industrial revolution."

The Planning Commission unanimously recommended approval in May 2025, but opposition grew at supervisors' meetings, where residents were already angry about the county's finances. Resident Doreen Billingsly said the county had no business doing deals like the data center if it could not handle its day-to-day business, according to meeting minutes. Nellie Turpin said the campus would be in the backyard of her home of more than 70 years, and others objected to noise, traffic, water and electricity use. The supervisors tabled the vote in June. On Aug. 18, 2025, Diode withdrew, saying it would "shift our focus elsewhere" based on the site's readiness for power and "municipal support," and indicated it would not resubmit. The county had already made data centers a permitted use in industrial zones in 2024, and the site sits in an area designated for development since 1979. What happens next: no new data center application in Charles City County has been publicly reported.
/data-centers/united-states/virginia/cha.unconfirmed: Whether the county has since received another data center proposal was not found; the reporting read is from 2025. The GovTech story is a syndicated (TNS) article; its original outlet was not named in the text read.
